Discretization bins:\n  - 0:  < -50 cm\n  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\n  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\n  - 3: 0 cm\n  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\n  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\n  - 6: > +50 cm\n- Absolute position in corridor, time-varying. Discretized into 5 equal-sized bins spanning the 450 cm track:\n  - 0: < 90 cm\n  - 1: 90 to 180 cm\n  - 2: 180 to 270 cm\n  - 3: 270 to 360 cm\n  - 4: > 360 cm\n- Speed, time-varying. Discretized into bins:\n  - 0: < 2 cm/s\n  - 1: 2-10 cm/s\n  - 2: 10-20 cm/s\n  - 3: 20-40 cm/s\n  - 4: > 40 cm/s\n- Lick, time-varying. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n- Reward zone location, per-trial. 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C\n- Reward outcome, per-trial. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n\n---\n\n## Conversion Workflow\n\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \n\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n2. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n\n---\n\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n  - Key decisions and rationale\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n  - Validation results and tables\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n  - Dataset description\n  - How to load and use the converted data\n  - Output format specification\n  - Key statistics\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n\n---\n\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. How is the `neural` data processed? \n\ni. dF/F is computed from F and Fneu and then deconvolved into \"events\", by a copy of the paper's own `preprocessing.dff`. Per plane: restrict to the lap samples (or lap plus teleport, depending on the session), subtract `0.7 * Fneu`, add each trial's mean neuropil back so the ratio is a true dF/F, take a maximin baseline (Gaussian smoothing with sigma 15 samples, then a 300-sample running minimum followed by a 300-sample running maximum, the Methods' 20 s window), form `(F - baseline)/|baseline|`, smooth with a 2-sample Gaussian, and deconvolve with OASIS at `tau = 0.7` and `frame_rate/n_planes`. Cells from multiple planes are pooled afterwards.\n\nWhether the baseline window may span the teleport is a per-mouse, per-day fact, copied from `teleport_metadata.py`: the laser was blanked between trials except on the days listed there, where imaging continued. It matters -- on m15 day 5, spanning the teleport widens the baseline window by 35% and moves the emitted events by ~9% (median per-cell r = 0.986).\n\nii.\n```python\ndff_curr, events_curr = dff(fluorescence_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n                            pd.Series(trial_start_idx + 1), pd.Series(trial_end_idx + 1),\n                            f_neu=neuropil_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n                            neuropil_method='subtract', baseline_method='maximin',\n                            subtract_baseline=True, neu_coef=0.7, tau=0.7,\n                            frame_rate=frame_rate, n_planes=nplanes, deconvolve=True,\n                            keep_teleports=keep_teleports)\n```\n\niii. This is the processing the Methods describe: \"baseline fluorescence was calculated within each trial independently using a maximin procedure with a 20 s sliding window ... dF/F was then calculated for each cell as the fluorescence minus the baseline, divided by the absolute value of the baseline, then smoothed with a two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel. The activity rate was extracted by deconvolving dF/F with a canonical calcium kernel using the OASIS algorithm as used in Suite2p.\" The parameters are theirs: `neu_coef = 0.7` and `baseline_method = 'maximin'` from `notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`, `tau = 0.7` from the suite2p ops in `notebooks/suite2p_notebooks/example_m12.ipynb`.\n\nThe neural sampling rate is the same for all recordings once the multi-plane sessions are accounted for. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n\ni. Derived from the `position` behavior time series and the reward zone location for the current trial. The reward zone boundaries come from the `reward_zone` behavior time series. This variable is non-zero when the mouse is in the reward zone. I combine this with the position of the mouse when this is non-zero to figure out the closest reward zone. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \n\nii. Assigning reward zone location for each trial: \n- Before converting, the `survey()` function was used to try to understand all the data values, including whatever is going on with the `reward_zone` variable. It first computes the position of the min and max position of the mouse when `reward_zone` is non-zero:\n```python\nbehavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series       \ninfo['reward_zone_positions'] = np.full((ntrials, 2), np.nan)\nposition = behavior_data['position'].data[:]\nfor trial in range(ntrials):\n    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n    pos_trial = position[idx]\n    reward_zone_trial = reward_zone[idx] > 0\n    if not np.any(reward_zone_trial):\n        continue\n    info['reward_zone_positions'][trial] = [np.min(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial]), np.max(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial])]\n```\nThe function `segment_reward_positions()` uses the Viterbi algorithm to assign reward zone labels so that the initial rewarded positions are close to the corresponding rewarded zone:\n```python\nreward_zone_dict = {'A': [80, 130],\n                    'B': [200, 250],\n                    'C': [320, 370]}\n...\nsigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\nzone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\ndist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n                    startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\ndist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\nlog_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n```\nIt also encourages the reward zone label to not change often:\n```python\npstay = .9\nlog_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\nnp.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n```\n\niii. The paper defines reward zones A, B, C at specific position ranges. These same ranges could also be found, with some translation, in the code (required mapping X -> A, etc.). I plotted the position of the mouse when `reward_zone` was positive (note that the value was between 0 and 6 I think) to determine that the Viterbi approach would likely work, and that the start of the rewarded position was the least noisy variable to use. The class fractions were approximately 1/3 after this, so it seemed correct. \n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. For each timepoint, compute the signed distance from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the reward zone. Distance is 0 when inside the zone, negative when before the zone, and positive when past it.  The continuous distance is then discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_distance_to_reward_zone(position_curr, reward_zone_curr):\n    ntimepoints = len(position_curr)\n    reward_zone_range = reward_zone_dict[reward_zone_curr]\n    distance_to_reward_zone = np.zeros(ntimepoints)\n    idx_before_zone = position_curr < reward_zone_range[0]\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_before_zone] = position_curr[idx_before_zone] - reward_zone_range[0]\n    idx_after_zone = position_curr > reward_zone_range[1]\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_after_zone] = position_curr[idx_after_zone] - reward_zone_range[1]\n    return distance_to_reward_zone\n\n```\n```python\ndistance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n```\n\n\niii. The reward zone boundaries are from `reward_zone_dict`, inspired by the reference code `Sosa_et_al_2024/src/reward_relative/behavior.py`. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n\n## 7-c. find nans\n99\t    nan_inds = np.isnan(a)\n100\t    a_nanless = np.copy(a)\n101\t    # make nans 0\n102\t    a_nanless[nan_inds] = 0\n103\t\n104\t    # inversely weight nanned indices\n105\t    one = np.ones(a.shape)\n106\t    one[nan_inds] = .001\n107\t    a_nanless = ndimage.gaussian_filter(a_nanless, sig) # was filters.gaussian_filter\n108\t    one = ndimage.gaussian_filter(one, sig) # was filters.gaussian_filter\n109\t    return a_nanless / one\n110\t\n111\t\n112\tdef nansmooth_1d(a, sig, axis=-1, return_nans=False, **kwargs):\n113\t    \"\"\"\n114\t    apply Gaussian smoothing to matrix A containing nans with kernel sig\n115\t    without propagating nans\n116\t    :param a:\n117\t    :param sig:\n118\t    :return:\n119\t\n120\t    ** copied from src/reward_relative/utilities.py::nansmooth **\n121\t    (renamed: the TwoPUtils N-D version above already occupies the name `nansmooth`)\n122\t    \"\"\"\n123\t\n124\t    # find nans\n125\t    nan_inds = np.isnan(a)\n126\t    a_nanless = np.copy(a)\n127\t    # make nans 0\n128\t    a_nanless[nan_inds] = 0\n129\t\n130\t    # inversely weight nanned indices\n131\t    one = np.ones(a.shape)\n132\t    one[nan_inds] = 0.001\n133\t    a_nanless = ndimage.gaussian_filter1d(a_nanless, sig, axis=axis, **kwargs) # Note that the threshold\n281\t        defaulted to 0.3 in the source function; the analyses always pass 0.5.\n282\t    :return: is_int (array) with a Boolean for each ROI, where putative interneuron is True.\n283\t\n284\t    ** copied from src/reward_relative/spatial.py::is_putative_interneuron **\n285\t    Change: takes the dF/F and speed arrays as arguments instead of reading them off a TwoPUtils \n286\t    `sess` object, which this conversion does not build.\n287\t    \"\"\"\n288\t    speed_corr = np.zeros((dff.shape[0],))\n289\t    nanmask = ~np.isnan(dff[0, :])\n290\t\n291\t    for c in range(dff.shape[0]):\n292\t        speed_corr[c] = np.corrcoef(\n293\t            dff[c, nanmask], speed[nanmask])[0, 1]\n294\t\n295\t    is_int = speed_corr > r_thresh\n296\t\n297\t    return is_int\n298\t\n299\t# end copy-paste\n300\t# =================================================================================================\n301\t\n302\t\n303\tdef get_subjects(datadir=DATADIR):\n304\t    # viterbi algorithm with a high cost for switching to encourage stable assignments\n775\t    zone_names = sorted(reward_zone_dict.keys())\n776\t    n_states = len(zone_names)\n777\t    zone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\n778\t    pstay = .9\n779\t    sigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\n780\t\n781\t    # transition log-probabilities\n782\t    log_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\n783\t    np.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n784\t\n785\t    results = {}\n786\t\n787\t    for mouse_id, positions in reward_zone_positions.items():\n788\t        n_trials = positions.shape[0]\n789\t        startpoints = positions[:,0] # use the start point as it looks cleaner\n790\t        valid = ~np.isnan(startpoints)\n791\t\n792\t        # emission log-probabilities: Gaussian penalty based on distance to zone range\n793\t        # distance is 0 if inside [lo, hi], otherwise distance to nearest edge\n794\t        # for NaN trials, uniform emission (all zeros) so assignment is driven by transitions\n795\t        log_emission = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\n796\t        dist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n797\t                          startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\n798\t        dist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\n799\t        log_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n800\t\n801\t        # viterbi forward pass\n802\t        log_delta = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\n803\t        psi = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states), dtype=int)\n804\t        log_delta[0] = log_emission[0]  # uniform prior\n805\t        for t in range(1, n_trials):\n806\t            for k in range(n_states):\n807\t                scores = log_delta[t - 1] + log_trans[:, k]\n808\t                psi[t, k] = np.argmax(scores)\n809\t                log_delta[t, k] = scores[psi[t, k]] + log_emission[t, k]\n810\t\n811\t        # backtrack\n812\t        states = np.zeros(n_trials, dtype=int)\n813\t        states[-1] = np.argmax(log_delta[-1])\n814\t        for t in range(n_trials - 2, -1, -1):\n815\t            states[t] = psi[t + 1, states[t + 1]]\n816\t\n817\t        # convert state indices to zone names\n818\t        zone_labels = np.array([zone_names[s] for s in states])\n819\t\n820\t        # distance from each trial's startpoint to its assigned zone range\n821\t        assigned_lo = zone_ranges[states, 0]\n822\t        assigned_hi = zone_ranges[states, 1]\n823\t        zone_dist = np.maximum(np.maximum(assigned_lo - startpoints, startpoints - assigned_hi), 0)\n824\t        zone_dist[~valid] = np.nan\n825\t\n826\t        results[mouse_id] = {'zone_labels': zone_labels, 'states': states, 'zone_dist': zone_dist}\n827\t\n828\t    return results\n829\t    \n830\t\n831\tdef main():\n832\t\n833\t all_info\n\ndef segment_reward_positions(reward_zone_positions):\n    # assign each trial to one of the reward zones defined in reward_zone_dict\n    # use viterbi algorithm with a high cost for switching to encourage stable assignments\n    zone_names = sorted(reward_zone_dict.keys())\n    n_states = len(zone_names)\n    zone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\n    pstay = .9\n    sigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\n\n    # transition log-probabilities\n    log_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\n    np.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n\n    results = {}\n\n    for mouse_id, positions in reward_zone_positions.items():\n        n_trials = positions.shape[0]\n        startpoints = positions[:,0] # use the start point as it looks cleaner\n        valid = ~np.isnan(startpoints)\n\n        # emission log-probabilities: Gaussian penalty based on distance to zone range\n        # distance is 0 if inside [lo, hi], otherwise distance to nearest edge\n        # for NaN trials, uniform emission (all zeros) so assignment is driven by transitions\n        log_emission = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\n        dist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n                          startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\n        dist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\n        log_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n\n        # viterbi forward pass\n        log_delta = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\n        psi = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states), dtype=int)\n        log_delta[0] = log_emission[0]  # uniform prior\n        for t in range(1, n_trials):\n            for k in range(n_states):\n                scores = log_delta[t - 1] + log_trans[:, k]\n                psi[t, k] = np.argmax(scores)\n                log_delta[t, k] = scores[psi[t, k]] + log_emission[t, k]\n\n        # backtrack\n        states = np.zeros(n_trials, dtype=int)\n        states[-1] = np.argmax(log_delta[-1])\n        for t in range(n_trials - 2, -1, -1):\n            states[t] = psi[t + 1, states[t + 1]]\n\n        # convert state indices to zone names\n        zone_labels = np.array([zone_names[s] for s in states])\n\n        # distance from each trial's startpoint to its assigned zone range\n        assigned_lo = zone_ranges[states, 0]\n        assigned_hi = zone_ranges[states, 1]\n        zone_dist = np.maximum(np.maximum(assigned_lo - startpoints, startpoints - assigned_hi), 0)\n        zone_dist[~valid] = np.nan\n\n        results[mouse_id] = {'zone_labels': zone_labels, 'states': states, 'zone_dist': zone_dist}\n\n    return results\n [trial_start_inds[t], teleport_inds[t])  (behavior.* convention)\n  * trial curation : lick-sensor-error trials removed\n                     -> behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error, correction_thr=0.3\n  * reward zones   : behavior.get_reward_zones (scene name + switch after 30 trials)\n  * reward outcome : behavior.get_trial_types (any(reward) and any(rzone))\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport glob\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport sys\nimport time\nimport warnings\nfrom multiprocessing import Pool\n\nimport h5py\nimport numpy as np\nimport scipy.ndimage as ndi\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Constants taken from the reference code / Methods\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nDATA_ROOT = '/app/data'\n\n# reward_relative.behavior.reward_zone_dict, via map_labels A->X, B->Y, C->Z\nREWARD_ZONE_COORDS = {'A': (80.0, 130.0), 'B': (200.0, 250.0), 'C': (320.0, 370.0)}\n\nCHANGE_TRIAL = 30          # behavior.get_reward_zones default; \"each switch occurred after 30 trials\"\nNEU_COEF = 0.7             # preprocessing.dff / utilities.default_dff_method\nBASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 15  # frames, nansmooth(f_, [0, 15]) in preprocessing.dff\nBASELINE_FILTER_WIN = 300  # frames, ~20 s minimum/maximum filter (\"maximin\")\nDFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 2       # frames, \"two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel\"\nINTERNEURON_R_THRESH = 0.5  # dayData.int_thresh\nLICK_CORRECTION_THR = 0.3  # Methods: \">30% of the ... samples ... cumulative lick count >2\"\n\nTRACK_LENGTH = 450.0\nN_POSITION_BINS = 5        # decoder task: 5 equal bins over the 450 cm track\nSPEED_BIN_EDGES = [2.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0]\n\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_trial_start', 'environment', 'trial_number', 'prev_trial_outcome']\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['reward_zone_distance', 'position', 'speed', 'lick',\n                'reward_zone_location', 'reward_outcome']\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['< -50 cm', '-50 to -10 cm', '-10 to <0 cm', '0 cm (in zone)',\n     '>0 to +10 cm', '+10 to +50 cm', '> +50 cm'],\n    ['< 90 cm', '90-180 cm', '180-270 cm', '270-360 cm', '> 360 cm'],\n    ['< 2 cm/s', '2-10 cm/s', '10-20 cm/s', '20-40 cm/s', '> 40 cm/s'],\n    ['no lick', 'lick'],\n    ['zone A (80-130 cm)', 'zone B (200-250 cm)', 'zone C (320-370 cm)'],\n    ['omitted', 'rewarded'],\n]\n\nBEHAVIOR_PATH = 'processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries'\nOPHYS_PATH = 'processing/ophys'\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Reference-code helpers\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\ndef get_reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials, change_trial=CHANGE_TRIAL):\n    \"\"\"Per-trial reward zone label ('A'/'B'/'C'), replicating behavior.get_reward_zones.\n\n    Non-switch scenes end in 'LocationX'; switch scenes contain '<first>_to' and end\n    with the second zone letter (e.g. 'Env1_LocationB_to_A', 'Env1_B_to_Env2_C').\n    \"\"\"\n    for lab in 'ABC':\n        if scene.endswith('Location' + lab):\n            return np.array([lab] * ntrials)\n    for first in 'ABC':\n        if f'{first}_to' in scene:\n            second = scene[-1]\n            if second not in 'ABC':\n                break\n            n0 = min(change_trial, ntrials)\n            return np.array([first] * n0 + [second] * (ntrials - n0))\n    raise NotImplementedError(f'Reward zones not defined for scene {scene}')\n\n\ndef nan_gaussian_filter1d(a, sigma, axis=-1):\n    \"\"\"utilities.nansmooth / TwoPUtils.utilities.nansmooth.\n\n    Within a trial slice there are never NaNs, so this reduces exactly to\n    scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter1d (the weight array is all ones and the\n    normalisation is 1 everywhere).\n    \"\"\"\n    return ndi.gaussian_filter1d(a, sigma, axis=axis)\n\n\ndef compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops):\n    \"\"\"dF/F per trial, replicating reward_relative.preprocessing.dff.\n\n    Reference call (utilities.multi_anim_sess, single-channel branch):\n        pp.dff(F, trial_starts, teleports, f_neu=Fneu, neuropil_method='subtract',\n               baseline_method='maximin', subtract_baseline=True, regress_ts=None,\n               neu_coef=0.7, keep_teleports=False)\n    which slices each trial as [start-1, stop-1).  We pass starts+1/stops+1 so the\n    sliced window is exactly [trial_start, teleport), matching every behavioural\n    function in the reference.\n\n    Args:\n        F, Fneu: (ncells, nframes) float arrays (raw fluorescence and neuropil)\n        starts, stops: (ntrials,) int arrays; trial t is [starts[t], stops[t])\n\n    Returns:\n        list of (ncells, T_t) float32 dF/F arrays, one per trial\n    \"\"\"\n    out = []\n    for s, e in zip(starts, stops):\n        f = F[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n        fneu = Fneu[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n\n        # neuropil subtraction, then add back the trial's mean neuropil so that the\n        # baseline is not a near-zero number (preprocessing.dff)\n        f = f - NEU_COEF * fneu\n        f = f + NEU_COEF * np.mean(fneu, axis=1, keepdims=True)\n\n        # \"maximin\" baseline: smooth, minimum-filter over ~20 s, then maximum-filter\n        flow = nan_gaussian_filter1d(f, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n\n        dff = (f - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        dff = nan_gaussian_filter1d(dff, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        out.append(dff.astype(np.float32))\n    return out\n\n\ndef find_putative_interneurons(dff_trials, speed_trials, r_thresh=INTERNEURON_R_THRESH):\n    \"\"\"spatial.is_putative_interneuron(method='speed'): Pearson r(dF/F, speed) > thresh.\n\n    The reference correlates the whole dF/F timeseries against speed over the samples\n    where dF/F is not NaN, which is exactly the union of the trial windows.  Computed\n    here from per-trial accumulators to avoid materialising the concatenation.\n    \"\"\"\n    ncells = dff_trials[0].shape[0]\n    n = 0\n    sx = np.zeros(ncells)\n    sxx = np.zeros(ncells)\n    sxy = np.zeros(ncells)\n    sy = 0.0\n    syy = 0.0\n    for d, v in zip(dff_trials, speed_trials):\n        d64 = d.astype(np.float64)\n        n += d64.shape[1]\n        sx += d64.sum(axis=1)\n        sxx += np.einsum('ij,ij->i', d64, d64)\n        sxy += d64 @ v\n        sy += v.sum()\n        syy += v @ v\n    cov = sxy - sx * sy / n\n    vx = sxx - sx ** 2 / n\n    vy = syy - sy ** 2 / n\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n        r = cov / np.sqrt(vx * vy)\n    return np.nan_to_num(r, nan=0.0) > r_thresh, r\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Output discretisation (decoder task specification)\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\ndef bin_reward_distance(dist):\n    \"\"\"0: <-50 | 1: [-50,-10) | 2: [-10,0) | 3: 0 | 4: (0,10] | 5: (10,50] | 6: >50\"\"\"\n    b = np.zeros(dist.shape, dtype=np.int8)\n    b[(dist >= -50) & (dist < -10)] = 1\n    b[(dist >= -10) & (dist < 0)] = 2\n    b[dist == 0] = 3\n    b[(dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)] = 4\n    b[(dist > 10) & (dist <= 50)] = 5\n    b[dist > 50] = 6\n    return b\n\n\ndef bin_position(pos):\n    \"\"\"5 equal bins spanning the 450 cm track (90 cm each).\"\"\"\n    b = np.floor(pos / (TRACK_LENGTH / N_POSITION_BINS))\n    return np.clip(b, 0, N_POSITION_BINS - 1).astype(np.int8)\n\n\ndef bin_speed(speed):\n    \"\"\"0: <2 | 1: 2-10 | 2: 10-20 | 3: 20-40 | 4: >40 cm/s\"\"\"\n    return np.digitize(speed, SPEED_BIN_EDGES).astype(np.int8)\n\n\ndef reward_zone_distance(pos, lo, hi):\n    \"\"\"Signed distance to the nearest point of the reward zone; 0 inside the zone.\"\"\"\n    return np.where(pos < lo, pos - lo, np.where(pos > hi, pos - hi, 0.0))\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Per-session conversion\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\ndef read_behavior(f):\n    \"\"\"Read the behavioural streams and the trial boundaries from an open NWB file.\"\"\"\n    B = f[BEHAVIOR_PATH]\n    beh = {k: B[f'{k}/data'][:] for k in\n           ['position', 'speed', 'lick', 'reward_zone', 'environment',\n            'trial_start', 'teleport', 'scanning']}\n    beh['time'] = B['position/timestamps'][:]\n\n    # Reward is stored as an event series; map each event back onto its imaging frame\n    # to recover the per-frame binary vr_data['reward'] the reference code uses.\n    rt = B['Reward/timestamps'][:]\n    ts = beh['time']\n    idx = np.clip(np.searchsorted(ts, rt), 0, len(ts) - 1)\n    left = np.clip(idx - 1, 0, len(ts) - 1)\n    idx = np.where(np.abs(ts[left] - rt) < np.abs(ts[idx] - rt), left, idx)\n    reward = np.zeros(len(ts))\n    reward[idx] = 1.0\n    beh['reward'] = reward\n\n    starts = np.where(beh['trial_start'] > 0)[0]\n    stops = np.where(beh['teleport'] > 0)[0]\n    assert len(starts) == len(stops) and np.all(stops > starts), 'bad trial boundaries'\n    return beh, starts, stops\n\n\ndef read_fluorescence(f):\n    \"\"\"Pooled (ncells, nframes) F and Fneu over all imaging planes, iscell-curated.\"\"\"\n    seg = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation']\n    iscell = seg['iscell'][:, 0] > 0\n    planes = sorted(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence'].keys(),\n                    key=lambda p: int(p.replace('plane', '')))\n    Fs, Ns = [], []\n    for p in planes:\n        rois = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/rois'][:]\n        keep = iscell[rois]\n        Fs.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n        Ns.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Neuropil/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n    F = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Fs, axis=1).T)\n    Fneu = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Ns, axis=1).T)\n    return F, Fneu, int(iscell.sum()), len(planes)\n\n\ndef convert_session(path, show_processing=False, outdir='/app'):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB session. Returns a dict with per-trial neural/input/output.\"\"\"\n    t0 = time.time()\n    timing = {}\n    with h5py.File(path, 'r') as f:\n        beh, starts, stops = read_behavior(f)\n        scene = f['identifier'][()].decode().split('/')[-1]\n        subject = f['general/subject/subject_id'][()].decode()\n        session_id = f['general/session_id'][()].decode()\n        region = f['general/optophysiology/ImagingPlane/location'][()].decode()\n        # ImagingPlane/imaging_rate is the total scan rate (31.0 Hz for the two\n        # 2-plane mice m17/m18); the effective per-plane sampling rate -- which is\n        # what every timeseries in the file is sampled at -- is 15.5078125 Hz for\n        # every session.  Derive it from the frame timestamps.\n        frame_rate = float(1.0 / np.median(np.diff(beh['time'])))\n        t1 = time.time()\n        timing['read_behavior'] = t1 - t0\n        F, Fneu, n_iscell, nplanes = read_fluorescence(f)\n    t2 = time.time()\n    timing['read_fluorescence'] = t2 - t1\n\n    ntrials = len(starts)\n\n    # ---- per-trial behaviour -----------------------------------------------------\n    pos_tr = [beh['position'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    speed_tr = [beh['speed'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    lick_tr = [beh['lick'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    rz_tr = [beh['reward_zone'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    rew_tr = [beh['reward'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    env_tr = [beh['environment'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    time_tr = [beh['time'][s:e] - beh['time'][s] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n\n    # behavior.get_trial_types\n    isreward = np.array([float(np.any(r > 0) and np.any(z > 0))\n                         for r, z in zip(rew_tr, rz_tr)])\n    env = np.array([np.unique(e)[0] for e in env_tr])\n    for e in env_tr:\n        assert len(np.unique(e)) == 1, 'environment changes within a trial'\n\n    # behavior.get_reward_zones\n    labels = get_reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials)\n\n    # behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error -> trials to drop\n    lick_error = np.array([(l > 2).sum() / len(l) > LICK_CORRECTION_THR for l in lick_tr])\n\n    # ---- neural ------------------------------------------------------------------\n    dff_trials = compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops)\n    t3 = time.time()\n    timing['dff'] = t3 - t2\n\n    is_int, speed_r = find_putative_interneurons(dff_trials, [v.astype(np.float64)\n                                                             for v in speed_tr])\n    keep_cells = ~is_int\n    dff_trials = [d[keep_cells] for d in dff_trials]\n    t4 = time.time()\n    timing['interneurons'] = t4 - t3\n\n    n_nonfinite = int(sum(np.sum(~np.isfinite(d)) for d in dff_trials))\n    if n_nonfinite:\n        warnings.warn(f'{os.path.basename(path)}: {n_nonfinite} ----------------------------------------------------------------\n    neural, inputs, outputs, kept_trials = [], [], [], []\n    for t in range(ntrials):\n        if lick_error[t]:\n            continue\n        T = len(pos_tr[t])\n        lo, hi = REWARD_ZONE_COORDS[labels[t]]\n        dist = reward_zone_distance(pos_tr[t], lo, hi)\n\n        inp = np.empty((4, T), dtype=np.float32)\n        inp[0] = time_tr[t]\n        inp[1] = env[t]\n        inp[2] = t                                  # original index within the session\n        inp[3] = isreward[t - 1] if t > 0 else 0.0  # no known preceding lap for trial 0\n\n        out = np.empty((6, T), dtype=np.int8)\n        out[0] = bin_reward_distance(dist)\n        out[1] = bin_position(pos_tr[t])\n        out[2] = inputs.append(inp)\n        outputs.append(out)\n        kept_trials.append(t)\n\n    timing['total'] = time.time() - t0\n    info = dict(\n        path=path, subject=subject, session_id=session_id, scene=scene,\n        region=region, frame_rate=frame_rate, nplanes=nplanes,\n        n_iscell=n_iscell, n_interneurons=int(is_int.sum()),\n        nneurons=int(keep_cells.sum()), ntrials_raw=ntrials,\n        ntrials=len(neural), n_lick_error=int(lick_error.sum()),\n        n_nonfinite=n_nonfinite, kept_trials=kept_trials,\n        reward_rate=float(isreward.mean()), timing=timing,\n    )\n\n    if show_processing:\n        plot_processing(path, beh, starts, stops, F, Fneu, dff_trials, keep_cells,\n                        labels, isreward, env, lick_error, neural, inputs, outputs,\n                        kept_trials, info, outdir)\n\n    return dict(neural=neural, input=inputs, output=outputs, info=info)\n\n\n# Manual curation eliminated ROIs containing multiple somata or dendrites, lacking visually obvious transients, suspected of overexpressing the calcium indicator or exhibiting high and continuous fluorescence fluctuation typical of putative interneurons. This approach yielded 155–2172 putative pyramidal neurons per session, owing to variation in imaging window implant quality and viral expression. In multi-plane imaged animals (see ‘2P imaging’), ROIs were identified separately per plane, but planes were pooled for all analyses except those in Extended Data Fig. 7. Custom code was used to follow individual ROIs across imaging sessions using the intersection over union of their pixels. The threshold for ROI matching was chosen algorithmically for each dataset such that the intersection over union for the best match for an ROI pair was always greater than the intersection over union for any second-best match.\n29:To compute the ΔF/F (dF/F) for each ROI, baseline fluorescence was calculated within each trial independently using a maximin procedure with a 20 s sliding window. Limitation to individual trials both accounts for potential photobleaching over the session and avoids the teleport periods for sessions during which the laser power was reduced (see ‘2P imaging’). The value of dF/F was then calculated for each cell as the fluorescence minus the baseline, divided by the absolute value of the baseline, then smoothed with a two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel. The activity rate was extracted by deconvolving dF/F with a canonical calcium kernel using the OASIS algorithm as used in Suite2p. We note that this deconvolution is not interpreted as a spike rate but rather as a method to eliminate the asymmetric smoothing of the calcium signal induced by indicator kinetics. Additional putative interneurons were detected for exclusion from further analysis by a Pearson correlation of >0.5 between their dF/F timeseries and the animal’s running speed, excluding 0.42 ± 0.85% of cells (mean ± s.d. across mice and days).\n53:For all neural spatial activity analyses, we excluded activity when the animal was moving at <2 cm s−1. To obtain an activity matrix of trials × position bins for each cell, we binned the 450 cm linear track into 45 bins of 10 cm each. We took the mean dF/F or deconvolved calcium activity on each trial within each position bin (note that taking the mean activity over time samples is equivalent to normalizing by the occupancy within a trial).\n55:We defined place cells as cells with significant SI65 in either trial set 1 (pre-reward-switch) or trial set 2 (post-reward-switch) in a session. On days without a switch, we used the first and second halves of trials. For the SI, we used the deconvolved calcium activity as this reduces the asymmetry of the calcium signal. SI was calculated for calcium imaging as:\n59:where pi is the occupancy probability in position bin i for the whole session, fi is the trial-averaged activity per position bin i and f is the mean activity over the whole session, computed as the sum of fi × pi over all N bins. To determine pi, we calculated the per-trial occupancy (number of imaging samples) in each bin divided by the total number of samples per trial, then summed the occupancy probabilities across trials and divided by the total per session. To determine the significance of the SI scores, we created a null distribution by circularly permuting the position data relative to the timeseries of each cell, by a random amount between ~1 s and the length of the trial, independently on each trial. SI was calculated from the trial-averaged activity of each shuffle, and this shuffle procedure was repeated 100 times per cell. A cell’s true SI was considered significant if it exceeded 95% of the SI scores from all shuffles within an animal, pooled across cells (more stringent than comparing to the shuffle of each individual cell). For plotting place cell firing over trials (for example, Fig. 2), deconvolved calcium activity was normalized to the mean of each cell within a session and smoothed with a 10 cm s.d. Gaussian.\n67:Correlation matrices were computed using the spatially binned deconvolved activity on each trial, smoothed with a 20 cm s.d. Gaussian for single cells and a 10 cm s.d. Gaussian for population vectors. This resulted in a matrix, A, of j trials × m position bins per cell. For population vectors, single-cell matrices were horizontally concatenated such that A was j trials × m position bins × n cells. Each trial was z-scored across the position axis. For single cells, the trial-by-trial correlation matrix C was computed as:\n79:For stringent statistics on putative RR remapping (Fig. 2c–i and Extended Data Fig. 2g–n), we restricted the set of included place cells to require significant SI in the pre-switch and post-switch trial sets in each session. We converted the position timeseries of the animal to periodic coordinates, setting 0 cm on the track to −π and 450 cm to π. Spatial peaks for each cell were re-computed using binned dF/F at a periodic bin size of 2π / 45 (corresponding to ~10 cm). Putative TR cells were removed by excluding cells with spatial peaks within ~0.698 radians (50 cm) of each other before versus after the switch. The periodic coordinates were then circularly rotated to align the start of each reward zone at 0, to measure the signed circular distance of spatial peaks relative to the start of each reward zone. For scatter plots of spatial peaks in Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 2, points are jittered by a random amount between −π / 100 and +π / 100 for visualization only. We measured the circularly wrapped difference between relative peaks after minus before the switch, creating a distribution that can be thought of as orthogonal to the unity line in Fig. 2d,f. We compared this distribution to a ‘random-remapping’ shuffle, generated by maintaining the pre-switch peak of each cell and circularly permuting its post-switch firing 1,000 times by a random offset of 0–44 bins. To define a candidate range of RR remapping variability, we computed the circular difference between the maximum and minimum bin of the distribution of true differences between RR peaks that exceeded the upper 95% of the shuffle, divided by two and averaged across switches. In an initial cohort of n = 7 mice, this produced a mean range of ±0.656 radians (~46.9 cm) around 0, which is captured by a 50 cm threshold given our 10 cm bin size. This threshold was subsequently used to identify candidate RR remapping cells (see below).\n93:Using the spatially binned, deconvolved activity smoothed with a 10 cm s.d. Gaussian, excluding activity from movement speeds <2 cm s−1, candidate place fields were identified as regions of ≥20 cm that exceeded 20% of the maximum of the trial-averaged activity19 (over the 30 pre-switch trials or the final 30 post-switch trials). To include a given field, the cell was required to be significantly active within the field boundaries in at least eight (>25%) of the 30 trials, where ‘significantly active’ was defined as the raw, un-binned deconvolved activity at those positions exceeding its mean +1 s.d. across the 30 trials. For analyses of place field properties before versus after a reward switch, cells were excluded that did not have significant SI or a significant field both before and after the switch. Note the reference only sets the\n*licks* of these trials to NaN; the AI removes the whole trial (neural and all other outputs) because\nNaN is not a legal categorical output.\n\nii.\n```python\nLICK_CORRECTION_THR = 0.3  # Methods: \">30% of the ... samples ... cumulative lick count >2\"\n...\n    # behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error -> trials to drop\n    lick_error = np.array([(l > 2).sum() / len(l) > LICK_CORRECTION_THR for l in lick_tr])\n...\n    for t in range(ntrials):\n        if lick_error[t]:\n            continue\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 5 and Step 3 curation rules: the Methods say \"n = 81 out of 12,376 trials\nremoved\"; the AI's threshold sweep (Step 4) gives 81 trials at thr 0.3, 69 at 0.35 and 44 at 0.5, so\n0.3 — the value quoted in the Methods — is used and reproduces the paper's number exactly. The notes\nexplicitly justify dropping rather than NaN-ing: \"the reference NaNs their licks; NaN is not\nrepresentable in a categorical output\".\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. The raw suite2p traces: `processing/ophys/Fluorescence/plane*/data` (F) and\n`processing/ophys/Neuropil/plane*/data` (Fneu), restricted to the `iscell`-curated ROIs and pooled\nacross imaging planes. The NWB `Deconvolved` array is explicitly **not** used.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef read_fluorescence(f):\n    \"\"\"Pooled (ncells, nframes) F and Fneu over all imaging planes, iscell-curated.\"\"\"\n    seg = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation']\n    iscell = seg['iscell'][:, 0] > 0\n    planes = sorted(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence'].keys(),\n                    key=lambda p: int(p.replace('plane', '')))\n    Fs, Ns = [], []\n    for p in planes:\n        rois = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/rois'][:]\n        keep = iscell[rois]\n        Fs.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n        Ns.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Neuropil/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n    F = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Fs, axis=1).T)\n    Fneu = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Ns, axis=1).T)\n    return F, Fneu, int(iscell.sum()), len(planes)\n```\n\niii. Step 4's discrepancy table: \"NWB `Deconvolved` has F-scale amplitudes (max 10976) and no NaNs\n⇒ suite2p `spks` from **raw F**\", i.e. not the events the paper computes from its own dF/F, so it is\ndiscarded and the signal is recomputed from F and Fneu with the reference's `preprocessing.dff`.\nPlanes are pooled because the Methods say \"planes were pooled for all analyses except those in\nExtended Data Fig. 7\".\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. The paper's dF/F pipeline is re-implemented per trial: subtract `0.7 × Fneu`, add back the trial's\nmean neuropil (×0.7) so the baseline is not near zero, compute a \"maximin\" baseline (Gaussian\nsmoothing with σ = 15 frames, then a 300-frame ≈20 s minimum filter followed by a 300-frame maximum\nfilter), form `(F − F0)/|F0|`, and smooth with a 2-frame s.d. Gaussian. **The result is stored as the\nneural signal; the OASIS deconvolution step that the paper applies afterwards is deliberately not\nrun.** The teleport periods are always excluded from the baseline (`keep_teleports = False` for every\nsession — the per-animal/per-day `teleport_metadata.teleport_sessions` table the reference's\n`make_multi_anim_sess` notebook uses is not applied). Non-finite dF/F values would be warned about and\nzeroed; none occurred in the full run.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops):\n    out = []\n    for s, e in zip(starts, stops):\n        f = F[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n        fneu = Fneu[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n\n        # neuropil subtraction, then add back the trial's mean neuropil so that the\n        # baseline is not a near-zero number (preprocessing.dff)\n        f = f - NEU_COEF * fneu\n        f = f + NEU_COEF * np.mean(fneu, axis=1, keepdims=True)\n\n        # \"maximin\" baseline: smooth, minimum-filter over ~20 s, then maximum-filter\n        flow = nan_gaussian_filter1d(f, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n\n        dff = (f - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        dff = nan_gaussian_filter1d(dff, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        out.append(dff.astype(np.float32))\n    return out\n```\n```python\nNEU_COEF = 0.7             # preprocessing.dff / utilities.default_dff_method\nBASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 15  # frames, nansmooth(f_, [0, 15]) in preprocessing.dff\nBASELINE_FILTER_WIN = 300  # frames, ~20 s minimum/maximum filter (\"maximin\")\nDFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 2       # frames, \"two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel\"\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 1 and Step 10 Check 3 difference 4: the dF/F arithmetic and constants are taken\nfrom `preprocessing.dff`/`utilities.multi_anim_sess`. Deconvolution is skipped on two grounds —\n(a) \"it needs the per-session suite2p `ops['tau']`, which is not present in the NWB export;\nintroducing a guessed kernel would be a worse match to the reference than using the dF/F the paper\nitself defines\", and (b) an explicit experiment (Step 8, `cache/compare_signal.py`) in which the\nsample was rebuilt with `dcnv.oasis(dff, 2000, tau=0.7, 15.5 Hz)` and re-decoded: dF/F gave the\nbetter validation balanced accuracy on 5 of 6 outputs (e.g. position 0.713 vs 0.547). Step 10\nCheck 2 also audits the dF/F distribution (per-session max |dF/F| median 4.88; 7 × 10⁻⁶ of values\nexceed 10, from cells whose maximin baseline lands near zero) and keeps them because the reference\n`dff` divides by `|F0|` with no guard.\n\n## 2-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Because `pp.dff` internally slices\n`start-1 : stop-1`, the notes state the intent to pass `starts+1/stops+1` so that the neural window is\nthe same sample range; in the actual implementation dF/F is computed directly on `[s, e)`, which is\nthe same window.\n\nii.\n```python\n    starts = np.where(beh['trial_start'] > 0)[0]\n    stops = np.where(beh['teleport'] > 0)[0]\n    assert len(starts) == len(stops) and np.all(stops > starts), 'bad trial boundaries'\n    return beh, starts, stops\n```\n```python\n    pos_tr = [beh['position'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    speed_tr = [beh['speed'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    ...\n    dff_trials = compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 2: \"Trial window = `[trial_start_idx, teleport_idx)` — exactly the on-track\nsamples, matching every behavioural function in the reference\". Step 10 Check 3 notes this\ndeliberately uses one window for both the neural and behavioural streams, removing the reference's\nown one-sample inconsistency between `pp.dff` and its behaviour functions, and validates the trial\ndefinition by reproducing the paper's lick-sensor-error count exactly (81 trials). The stored\n`trial number` series was not used for boundaries. (Independently verified here: both flags are\n0/1 impulses, and the resulting boundaries are identical to the human reference's rising-edge\ndetection, giving the same 12,216 raw trials.)\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. One trial filter: trials flagged by the paper's capacitive-lick-sensor error test are dropped\nentirely. A trial is flagged when more than 30 % of its frames have a cumulative lick count > 2\n(`behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error` with `correction_thr = 0.3`). 81 trials of 12,216 (0.66 %) are\nremoved, leaving 12,135. No other trial exclusions: the notes verify that no trial overlaps the\npre-sync frames (`scanning != 1`), that every trial has a single environment value, and that the\nshortest trial is 96 frames, so no minimum-length filter is applied. Note the reference only sets the\n*licks* of these trials to NaN; the AI removes the whole trial (neural and all other outputs) because\nNaN is not a legal categorical output.\n\nii.\n```python\nLICK_CORRECTION_THR = 0.3  # Methods: \">30% of the ... samples ... cumulative lick count >2\"\n...\n    # behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error -> trials to drop\n    lick_error = np.array([(l > 2).sum() / len(l) > LICK_CORRECTION_THR for l in lick_tr])\n...\n    for t in range(ntrials):\n        if lick_error[t]:\n            continue\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 5 and Step 3 curation rules: the Methods say \"n = 81 out of 12,376 trials\nremoved\"; the AI's threshold sweep (Step 4) gives 81 trials at thr 0.3, 69 at 0.35 and 44 at 0.5, so\n0.3 — the value quoted in the Methods — is used and reproduces the paper's number exactly. The notes\nexplicitly justify dropping rather than NaN-ing: \"the reference NaNs their licks; NaN is not\nrepresentable in a categorical output\".\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. Step 4's discrepancy table: \"NWB `Deconvolved` has F-scale amplitudes (max 10976) and no NaNs\n⇒ suite2p `spks` from **raw F**\", i.e. not the events the paper computes from its own dF/F, so it is\ndiscarded and the signal is recomputed from F and Fneu with the reference's `preprocessing.dff`.\nPlanes are pooled because the Methods say \"planes were pooled for all analyses except those in\nExtended Data Fig. 7\".\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. The paper's dF/F pipeline is re-implemented per trial: subtract `0.7 × Fneu`, add back the trial's\nmean neuropil (×0.7) so the baseline is not near zero, compute a \"maximin\" baseline (Gaussian\nsmoothing with σ = 15 frames, then a 300-frame ≈20 s minimum filter followed by a 300-frame maximum\nfilter), form `(F − F0)/|F0|`, and smooth with a 2-frame s.d. Gaussian. **The result is stored as the\nneural signal; the OASIS deconvolution step that the paper applies afterwards is deliberately not\nrun.** The teleport periods are always excluded from the baseline (`keep_teleports = False` for every\nsession — the per-animal/per-day `teleport_metadata.teleport_sessions` table the reference's\n`make_multi_anim_sess` notebook uses is not applied). Non-finite dF/F values would be warned about and\nzeroed; none occurred in the full run.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops):\n    out = []\n    for s, e in zip(starts, stops):\n        f = F[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n        fneu = Fneu[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n\n        # neuropil subtraction, then add back the trial's mean neuropil so that the\n        # baseline is not a near-zero number (preprocessing.dff)\n        f = f - NEU_COEF * fneu\n        f = f + NEU_COEF * np.mean(fneu, axis=1, keepdims=True)\n\n        # \"maximin\" baseline: smooth, minimum-filter over ~20 s, then maximum-filter\n        flow = nan_gaussian_filter1d(f, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n\n        dff = (f - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        dff = nan_gaussian_filter1d(dff, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        out.append(dff.astype(np.float32))\n    return out\n```\n```python\nNEU_COEF = 0.7             # preprocessing.dff / utilities.default_dff_method\nBASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 15  # frames, nansmooth(f_, [0, 15]) in preprocessing.dff\nBASELINE_FILTER_WIN = 300  # frames, ~20 s minimum/maximum filter (\"maximin\")\nDFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 2       # frames, \"two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel\"\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 1 and Step 10 Check 3 difference 4: the dF/F arithmetic and constants are taken\nfrom `preprocessing.dff`/`utilities.multi_anim_sess`. Deconvolution is skipped on two grounds —\n(a) \"it needs the per-session suite2p `ops['tau']`, which is not present in the NWB export;\nintroducing a guessed kernel would be a worse match to the reference than using the dF/F the paper\nitself defines\", and (b) an explicit experiment (Step 8, `cache/compare_signal.py`) in which the\nsample was rebuilt with `dcnv.oasis(dff, 2000, tau=0.7, 15.5 Hz)` and re-decoded: dF/F gave the\nbetter validation balanced accuracy on 5 of 6 outputs (e.g. position 0.713 vs 0.547). Step 10\nCheck 2 also audits the dF/F distribution (per-session max |dF/F| median 4.88; 7 × 10⁻⁶ of values\nexceed 10, from cells whose maximin baseline lands near zero) and keeps them because the reference\n`dff` divides by `|F0|` with no guard.\n\n## 2-c. No cross-session neuron\nalignment is attempted, so each session's neurons are independent.\n\nii.\n```python\nsession_id = f['general/session_id'][()].decode()\nscene = f['identifier'][()].decode().split('/')[-1]\n...\nresults.sort(key=lambda r: (int(r['info']['subject'][1:]), int(r['info']['session_id'])))\n```\n\niii. Step 9's consistency table checks 152 sessions, 12 for m11 and 14 for every other mouse,\nagainst the paper's statement that imaging ran 14 days per mouse except m11 (from day 3). Step 4\nresolves the paper's 12,376-trial figure as including m11's two unimaged behaviour-only days\n(12,376 − 12,216 = 160 = 2 × 80 trials).\n\n## 1-d. How are the data split into trials?\n\ni. A trial is the on-track lap `[trial_start_idx, teleport_idx)`: it starts at the sample where the\n`trial_start` flag is set and ends (exclusive) at the first sample where the `teleport` flag is set.\nBoth flags are read as \"any sample > 0\", and the code asserts that starts and stops pair up one-to-one\nand that every stop follows its start. This is the same window every behavioural function in the\nreference repo uses (`get_trial_types`, `lickrate_PETH`, `correct_lick_sensor_error` all slice\n`sess.trial_start_inds[t] : sess.teleport_inds[t]`). Because `pp.dff` internally slices\n`start-1 : stop-1`, the notes state the intent to pass `starts+1/stops+1` so that the neural window is\nthe same sample range; in the actual implementation dF/F is computed directly on `[s, e)`, which is\nthe same window.\n\nii.\n```python\n    starts = np.where(beh['trial_start'] > 0)[0]\n    stops = np.where(beh['teleport'] > 0)[0]\n    assert len(starts) == len(stops) and np.all(stops > starts), 'bad trial boundaries'\n    return beh, starts, stops\n```\n```python\n    pos_tr = [beh['position'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    speed_tr = [beh['speed'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    ...\n    dff_trials = compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 2: \"Trial window = `[trial_start_idx, teleport_idx)` — exactly the on-track\nsamples, matching every behavioural function in the reference\". Step 10 Check 3 notes this\ndeliberately uses one window for both the neural and behavioural streams, removing the reference's\nown one-sample inconsistency between `pp.dff` and its behaviour functions, and validates the trial\ndefinition by reproducing the paper's lick-sensor-error count exactly (81 trials). The stored\n`trial number` series was not used for boundaries. (Independently verified here: both flags are\n0/1 impulses, and the resulting boundaries are identical to the human reference's rising-edge\ndetection, giving the same 12,216 raw trials.)\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. One trial filter: trials flagged by the paper's capacitive-lick-sensor error test are dropped\nentirely. A trial is flagged when more than 30 % of its frames have a cumulative lick count > 2\n(`behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error` with `correction_thr = 0.3`). 81 trials of 12,216 (0.66 %) are\nremoved, leaving 12,135. No other trial exclusions: the notes verify that no trial overlaps the\npre-sync frames (`scanning != 1`), that every trial has a single environment value, and that the\nshortest trial is 96 frames, so no minimum-length filter is applied. Note the reference only sets the\n*licks* of these trials to NaN; the AI removes the whole trial (neural and all other outputs) because\nNaN is not a legal categorical output.\n\nii.\n```python\nLICK_CORRECTION_THR = 0.3  # Methods: \">30% of the ... samples ... cumulative lick count >2\"\n...\n    # behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error -> trials to drop\n    lick_error = np.array([(l > 2).sum() / len(l) > LICK_CORRECTION_THR for l in lick_tr])\n...\n    for t in range(ntrials):\n        if lick_error[t]:\n            continue\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 5 and Step 3 curation rules: the Methods say \"n = 81 out of 12,376 trials\nremoved\"; the AI's threshold sweep (Step 4) gives 81 trials at thr 0.3, 69 at 0.35 and 44 at 0.5, so\n0.3 — the value quoted in the Methods — is used and reproduces the paper's number exactly. The notes\nexplicitly justify dropping rather than NaN-ing: \"the reference NaNs their licks; NaN is not\nrepresentable in a categorical output\".\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. The raw suite2p traces: `processing/ophys/Fluorescence/plane*/data` (F) and\n`processing/ophys/Neuropil/plane*/data` (Fneu), restricted to the `iscell`-curated ROIs and pooled\nacross imaging planes. The NWB `Deconvolved` array is explicitly **not** used.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef read_fluorescence(f):\n    \"\"\"Pooled (ncells, nframes) F and Fneu over all imaging planes, iscell-curated.\"\"\"\n    seg = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation']\n    iscell = seg['iscell'][:, 0] > 0\n    planes = sorted(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence'].keys(),\n                    key=lambda p: int(p.replace('plane', '')))\n    Fs, Ns = [], []\n    for p in planes:\n        rois = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/rois'][:]\n        keep = iscell[rois]\n        Fs.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n        Ns.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Neuropil/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n    F = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Fs, axis=1).T)\n    Fneu = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Ns, axis=1).T)\n    return F, Fneu, int(iscell.sum()), len(planes)\n```\n\niii. Step 4's discrepancy table: \"NWB `Deconvolved` has F-scale amplitudes (max 10976) and no NaNs\n⇒ suite2p `spks` from **raw F**\", i.e. not the events the paper computes from its own dF/F, so it is\ndiscarded and the signal is recomputed from F and Fneu with the reference's `preprocessing.dff`.\nPlanes are pooled because the Methods say \"planes were pooled for all analyses except those in\nExtended Data Fig. 7\".\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. The paper's dF/F pipeline is re-implemented per trial: subtract `0.7 × Fneu`, add back the trial's\nmean neuropil (×0.7) so the baseline is not near zero, compute a \"maximin\" baseline (Gaussian\nsmoothing with σ = 15 frames, then a 300-frame ≈20 s minimum filter followed by a 300-frame maximum\nfilter), form `(F − F0)/|F0|`, and smooth with a 2-frame s.d. Gaussian. **The result is stored as the\nneural signal; the OASIS deconvolution step that the paper applies afterwards is deliberately not\nrun.** The teleport periods are always excluded from the baseline (`keep_teleports = False` for every\nsession — the per-animal/per-day `teleport_metadata.teleport_sessions` table the reference's\n`make_multi_anim_sess` notebook uses is not applied). Non-finite dF/F values would be warned about and\nzeroed; none occurred in the full run.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops):\n    out = []\n    for s, e in zip(starts, stops):\n        f = F[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n        fneu = Fneu[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n\n        # neuropil subtraction, then add back the trial's mean neuropil so that the\n        # baseline is not a near-zero number (preprocessing.dff)\n        f = f - NEU_COEF * fneu\n        f = f + NEU_COEF * np.mean(fneu, axis=1, keepdims=True)\n\n        # \"maximin\" baseline: smooth, minimum-filter over ~20 s, then maximum-filter\n        flow = nan_gaussian_filter1d(f, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n\n        dff = (f - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        dff = nan_gaussian_filter1d(dff, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        out.append(dff.astype(np.float32))\n    return out\n```\n```python\nNEU_COEF = 0.7             # preprocessing.dff / utilities.default_dff_method\nBASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 15  # frames, nansmooth(f_, [0, 15]) in preprocessing.dff\nBASELINE_FILTER_WIN = 300  # frames, ~20 s minimum/maximum filter (\"maximin\")\nDFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 2       # frames, \"two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel\"\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 1 and Step 10 Check 3 difference 4: the dF/F arithmetic and constants are taken\nfrom `preprocessing.dff`/`utilities.multi_anim_sess`. Deconvolution is skipped on two grounds —\n(a) \"it needs the per-session suite2p `ops['tau']`, which is not present in the NWB export;\nintroducing a guessed kernel would be a worse match to the reference than using the dF/F the paper\nitself defines\", and (b) an explicit experiment (Step 8, `cache/compare_signal.py`) in which the\nsample was rebuilt with `dcnv.oasis(dff, 2000, tau=0.7, 15.5 Hz)` and re-decoded: dF/F gave the\nbetter validation balanced accuracy on 5 of 6 outputs (e.g. position 0.713 vs 0.547). Step 10\nCheck 2 also audits the dF/F distribution (per-session max |dF/F| median 4.88; 7 × 10⁻⁶ of values\nexceed 10, from cells whose maximin baseline lands near zero) and keeps them because the reference\n`dff` divides by `|F0|` with no guard.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters, both the paper's. First, ROIs are restricted to suite2p's manually curated cells\n(`PlaneSegmentation/iscell[:, 0] == 1`), applied per plane through each plane's `rois` index before\nthe traces are pooled. Second, putative interneurons are dropped: any cell whose dF/F correlates with\nrunning speed at Pearson r > 0.5, computed over all in-trial samples. 402 of 138,678 curated cells\n(0.29 %; 0.35 ± 0.61 % per session) are removed, leaving 138,276.\n\nii.\n```python\n    seg = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation']\n    iscell = seg['iscell'][:, 0] > 0\n    ...\n        rois = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/rois'][:]\n        keep = iscell[rois]\n```\n```python\ndef find_putative_interneurons(dff_trials, speed_trials, r_thresh=INTERNEURON_R_THRESH):\n    \"\"\"spatial.is_putative_interneuron(method='speed'): Pearson r(dF/F, speed) > thresh.\"\"\"\n    ...\n    for d, v in zip(dff_trials, speed_trials):\n        d64 = d.astype(np.float64)\n        n += d64.shape[1]\n        sx += d64.sum(axis=1); sxx += np.einsum('ij,ij->i', d64, d64); sxy += d64 @ v\n        sy += v.sum(); syy += v @ v\n    cov = sxy - sx * sy / n\n    ...\n    return np.nan_to_num(r, nan=0.0) > r_thresh, r\n...\n    is_int, speed_r = find_putative_interneurons(dff_trials, [v.astype(np.float64) for v in speed_tr])\n    keep_cells = ~is_int\n    dff_trials = [d[keep_cells] for d in dff_trials]\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. Signed distance from the animal's position to the nearest point of the active zone: negative before\nthe zone (`pos − lo`), positive after it (`pos − hi`), and exactly 0 anywhere inside. Computed\nvectorised over the trial, then discretised (7-c).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef reward_zone_distance(pos, lo, hi):\n    \"\"\"Signed distance to the nearest point of the reward zone; 0 inside the zone.\"\"\"\n    return np.where(pos < lo, pos - lo, np.where(pos > hi, pos - hi, 0.0))\n```\n\niii. The decoder task asks for \"distance to any location in the reward zone\", which the notes read as\n0 while the animal is anywhere in the 50 cm zone; the zone bounds are the paper's\n(A 80–130, B 200–250, C 320–370 cm). Step 9 sanity-checks the resulting class distribution: bin 3\n(\"0 cm\") holds 23.9 % of timepoints, consistent with the animal spending extra time in the zone (the\nzone is 50/450 ≈ 11 % of the track by length, but licking/slowing inflates the occupancy).\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Seven classes assigned by explicit boolean masks: 0 for < −50; 1 for [−50, −10); 2 for [−10, 0);\n3 for exactly 0 (inside the zone); 4 for (0, +10]; 5 for (+10, +50]; 6 for > +50 cm. Stored as int8.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_reward_distance(dist):\n    \"\"\"0: <-50 | 1: [-50,-10) | 2: [-10,0) | 3: 0 | 4: (0,10] | 5: (10,50] | 6: >50\"\"\"\n    b = np.zeros(dist.shape, dtype=np.int8)\n    b[(dist >= -50) & (dist < -10)] = 1\n    b[(dist >= -10) & (dist < 0)] = 2\n    b[dist == 0] = 3\n    b[(dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)] = 4\n    b[(dist > 10) & (dist <= 50)] = 5\n    b[dist > 50] = 6\n    return b\n```\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['< -50 cm', '-50 to -10 cm', '-10 to <0 cm', '0 cm (in zone)',\n     '>0 to +10 cm', '+10 to +50 cm', '> +50 cm'], ...\n```\n\niii. How is the `neural` data processed? \n\ni. dF/F is computed from F and Fneu and then deconvolved into \"events\", by a copy of the paper's own `preprocessing.dff`. Per plane: restrict to the lap samples (or lap plus teleport, depending on the session), subtract `0.7 * Fneu`, add each trial's mean neuropil back so the ratio is a true dF/F, take a maximin baseline (Gaussian smoothing with sigma 15 samples, then a 300-sample running minimum followed by a 300-sample running maximum, the Methods' 20 s window), form `(F - baseline)/|baseline|`, smooth with a 2-sample Gaussian, and deconvolve with OASIS at `tau = 0.7` and `frame_rate/n_planes`. Cells from multiple planes are pooled afterwards.\n\nWhether the baseline window may span the teleport is a per-mouse, per-day fact, copied from `teleport_metadata.py`: the laser was blanked between trials except on the days listed there, where imaging continued. It matters -- on m15 day 5, spanning the teleport widens the baseline window by 35% and moves the emitted events by ~9% (median per-cell r = 0.986).\n\nii.\n```python\ndff_curr, events_curr = dff(fluorescence_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n                            pd.Series(trial_start_idx + 1), pd.Series(trial_end_idx + 1),\n                            f_neu=neuropil_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n                            neuropil_method='subtract', baseline_method='maximin',\n                            subtract_baseline=True, neu_coef=0.7, tau=0.7,\n                            frame_rate=frame_rate, n_planes=nplanes, deconvolve=True,\n                            keep_teleports=keep_teleports)\n```\n\niii. This is the processing the Methods describe: \"baseline fluorescence was calculated within each trial independently using a maximin procedure with a 20 s sliding window ... dF/F was then calculated for each cell as the fluorescence minus the baseline, divided by the absolute value of the baseline, then smoothed with a two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel. The activity rate was extracted by deconvolving dF/F with a canonical calcium kernel using the OASIS algorithm as used in Suite2p.\" The parameters are theirs: `neu_coef = 0.7` and `baseline_method = 'maximin'` from `notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`, `tau = 0.7` from the suite2p ops in `notebooks/suite2p_notebooks/example_m12.ipynb`.\n\nThe neural sampling rate is the same for all recordings once the multi-plane sessions are accounted for. Note that the `rate` stored on the NWB series is the scanner rate, so on the two-plane sessions it is 31 Hz and the per-plane rate -- the one that sets both the time bin and the deconvolution kernel -- is `rate/nplanes`.\n\n## 2-c. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several cases are handled:\n- **Neural/behavior length mismatch**: If the number of neural time bins differs from behavior timestamps, data is cropped to the minimum of the two with a warning printed.\n- **Short trials**: Trials with fewer than 50 timepoints (`min_ntimepoints`) are skipped with a warning.\n- **Missing reward zone data**: Trials where `reward_zone` is never active (all zeros) get NaN positions, and the Viterbi algorithm handles these via uniform emission (assignment driven by neighboring trials' transitions).\n- **Reward timestamp alignment**: An assertion verifies reward times align within half a time bin of behavior timestamps.\n\nii.\n```python\nif T != len(timestamps):\n    print(f\"Warning: number of neural time bins ({T}) does not match number of behavior timestamps ({len(timestamps)}), cropping to the minimum of the two\")\n    T = min(T, len(timestamps))\n    spike_data = spike_data[:T]\n    timestamps = timestamps[:T]\n...\nif idx.sum() < min_ntimepoints:\n    print(f\"Skipping trial {trial}...\")\n    istrial[trial] = False\n    continue\n```\n\niii. These are defensive checks found during data exploration. The neural/behavior mismatch occurs in a small number of sessions.\n\n## 13-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. The most time-consuming steps are:\n1. **Loading NWB files** (`pynwb.NWBHDF5IO` and reading large arrays) — I/O bound\n2. **The survey step** — loads every NWB file to gather statistics and reward zone positions\n3. **Full conversion** — loads every NWB file again and extracts all trial data\n4. **Saving the .pkl file**\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The NWB files are large (contain full neural recordings). Conversion is otherwise quite fast\n\n## 13-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. The per-trial loop in `convert_session_data` (lines 267-332) iterates over each trial sequentially. Some operations like `np.digitize` and `compute_distance_to_reward_zone` could theoretically be applied to the full session arrays before splitting into trials, but the variable trial lengths make this awkward. The Viterbi inner loop (lines 503-507) iterates over states, which could be vectorized with matrix operations.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The per-trial loop is the natural structure given variable-length trials. Vectorizing would require padding or masking.\n\n## 13-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. The survey step and the conversion step both load every NWB file and read the same data arrays (neural, behavior). The survey reads neural data to count neurons and check rates, then the conversion reads it again. The `reward_zone_positions` are computed in the survey and then used in the conversion, but other data (position, speed, lick, etc.) is read twice. \n\nii. N/A\n\niii. I don't think these could be run at the same time, as it would require too much RAM. The Viterbi output created during surveying is required to process the data. It was convenient to run the survey before deciding how to handle the conversion of the data. \n\n## 13-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\ni. N/A\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 13-e. How is memory usage optimized?\n\ni. N/A\n\nii. N/A\n\niii.
