find nans\n    nan_inds = np.isnan(a)\n    a_nanless = np.copy(a)\n    # make nans 0\n    a_nanless[nan_inds] = 0\n\n    # inversely weight nanned indices\n    one = np.ones(a.shape)\n    one[nan_inds] = .001\n    a_nanless = ndimage.gaussian_filter(a_nanless, sig) # was filters.gaussian_filter\n    one = ndimage.gaussian_filter(one, sig) # was filters.gaussian_filter\n    return a_nanless / one\n\n\ndef nansmooth_1d(a, sig, axis=-1, return_nans=False, **kwargs):\n    \"\"\"\n    apply Gaussian smoothing to matrix A containing nans with kernel sig\n    without propagating nans\n    :param a:\n    :param sig:\n    :return:\n\n    ** copied from src/reward_relative/utilities.py::nansmooth **\n    (renamed: the TwoPUtils N-D version above already occupies the name `nansmooth`)\n    \"\"\"\n\n    # find nans\n    nan_inds = np.isnan(a)\n    a_nanless = np.copy(a)\n    # make nans 0\n    a_nanless[nan_inds] = 0\n\n    # inversely weight nanned indices\n    one = np.ones(a.shape)\n    one[nan_inds] = 0.001\n    a_nanless = ndimage.gaussian_filter1d(a_nanless, sig, axis=axis, **kwargs) # was filters.gaussian_filter\n    one = ndimage.gaussian_filter1d(one, sig, axis=axis, **kwargs) # was filters.gaussian_filter\n\n    out = a_nanless / one\n    if return_nans:\n        out[nan_inds] = np.nan\n\n    return out\n\ndef dff(f,\n        trial_starts,\n        teleports,\n        f_neu=None,\n        neuropil_method=None,\n        baseline_method='maximin',\n        subtract_baseline=True,\n        neu_coef=0.7,\n        tau=0.7,\n        frame_rate=15,\n        n_planes=1,\n        deconvolve=False,\n        keep_teleports=False):\n    \"\"\"\n    Calculate dFF for 1 channel\n\n    :param f: ROI fluorescence timeseries\n    :param trial_starts:\n    :param teleports:\n    :param f_neu: neuropil fluorescence timeseries\n    :param baseline_method:\n    :param subtract_baseline: True gives ∆F/F, False just normalizes F to the basline (divides only)\n    :param neu_coef:\n    :param deconvolve: whether to deconvolve the dff trace into \"events\" (psuedo spikes)\n    :return: dff and spks if deconvolve is True, otherwise just dff\n\n    `trial_starts` and `teleports` must be pandas Series: the keep_teleports branch calls\n    `.to_list()` on `teleports`, which a numpy array does not have. We pass starts+1/stops+1 so the\n    sliced window is exactly [trial_start, teleport), matching every behavioural\n    function in the reference.\n\n    Args:\n        F, Fneu: (ncells, nframes) float arrays (raw fluorescence and neuropil)\n        starts, stops: (ntrials,) int arrays; trial t is [starts[t], stops[t])\n\n    Returns:\n        list of (ncells, T_t) float32 dF/F arrays, one per trial\n    \"\"\"\n    out = []\n    for s, e in zip(starts, stops):\n        f = F[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n        fneu = Fneu[:, s:e].astype(np.float64)\n\n        # neuropil subtraction, then add back the trial's mean neuropil so that the\n        # baseline is not a near-zero number (preprocessing.dff)\n        f = f - NEU_COEF * fneu\n        f = f + NEU_COEF * np.mean(fneu, axis=1, keepdims=True)\n\n        # \"maximin\" baseline: smooth, minimum-filter over ~20 s, then maximum-filter\n        flow = nan_gaussian_filter1d(f, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        flow = ndi.maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n\n        dff = (f - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        dff = nan_gaussian_filter1d(dff, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=-1)\n        out.append(dff.astype(np.float32))\n    return out\n\n\ndef find_putative_interneurons(dff_trials, speed_trials, r_thresh=INTERNEURON_R_THRESH):\n    \"\"\"spatial.is_putative_interneuron(method='speed'): Pearson r(dF/F, speed) > thresh.\n\n    The reference correlates the whole dF/F timeseries against speed over the samples\n    where dF/F is not NaN, which is exactly the union of the trial windows.  Computed\n    here from per-trial accumulators to avoid materialising the concatenation.\n    \"\"\"\n    ncells = dff_trials[0].shape[0]\n    n = 0\n    sx = np.zeros(ncells)\n    sxx = np.zeros(ncells)\n    sxy = np.zeros(ncells)\n    sy = 0.0\n    syy = 0.0\n    for d, v in zip(dff_trials, speed_trials):\n        d64 = d.astype(np.float64)\n        n += d64.shape[1]\n        sx += d64.sum(axis=1)\n        sxx += np.einsum('ij,ij->i', d64, d64)\n        sxy += d64 @ v\n        sy += v.sum()\n        syy += v @ v\n    cov = sxy - sx * sy / n\n    vx = sxx - sx ** 2 / n\n    vy = syy - sy ** 2 / n\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n        r = cov / np.sqrt(vx * vy)\n    return np.nan_to_num(r, nan=0.0) > r_thresh, r\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Output discretisation (decoder task specification)\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\ndef bin_reward_distance(dist):\n    \"\"\"0: <-50 | 1: [-50,-10) | 2: [-10,0) | 3: 0 | 4: (0,10] | 5: (10,50] | 6: >50\"\"\"\n    b = np.zeros(dist.shape, dtype=np.int8)\n    b[(dist >= -50) & (dist < -10)] = 1\n    b[(dist >= -10) & (dist < 0)] = 2\n    b[dist == 0] = 3\n    b[(dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)] = 4\n    b[(dist > 10) & (dist <= 50)] = 5\n    b[dist > 50] = 6\n    return b\n\n\ndef bin_position(pos):\n    \"\"\"5 equal bins spanning the 450 cm track (90 cm each).\"\"\"\n    b = np.floor(pos / (TRACK_LENGTH / N_POSITION_BINS))\n    return np.clip(b, 0, N_POSITION_BINS - 1).astype(np.int8)\n\n\ndef bin_speed(speed):\n    \"\"\"0: <2 | 1: 2-10 | 2: 10-20 | 3: 20-40 | 4: >40 cm/s\"\"\"\n    return np.digitize(speed, SPEED_BIN_EDGES).astype(np.int8)\n\n\ndef reward_zone_distance(pos, lo, hi):\n    \"\"\"Signed distance to the nearest point of the reward zone; 0 inside the zone.\"\"\"\n    return np.where(pos < lo, pos - lo, np.where(pos > hi, pos - hi, 0.0))\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Per-session conversion\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\ndef read_behavior(f):\n    \"\"\"Read the behavioural streams and the trial boundaries from an open NWB file.\"\"\"\n    B = f[BEHAVIOR_PATH]\n    beh = {k: B[f'{k}/data'][:] for k in\n           ['position', 'speed', 'lick', 'reward_zone', 'environment',\n            'trial_start', 'teleport', 'scanning']}\n    beh['time'] = B['position/timestamps'][:]\n\n    # Reward is stored as an event series; map each event back onto its imaging frame\n    # to recover the per-frame binary vr_data['reward'] the reference code uses.\n    rt = B['Reward/timestamps'][:]\n    ts = beh['time']\n    idx = np.clip(np.searchsorted(ts, rt), 0, len(ts) - 1)\n    left = np.clip(idx - 1, 0, len(ts) - 1)\n    idx = np.where(np.abs(ts[left] - rt) < np.abs(ts[idx] - rt), left, idx)\n    reward = np.zeros(len(ts))\n    reward[idx] = 1.0\n    beh['reward'] = reward\n\n    starts = np.where(beh['trial_start'] > 0)[0]\n    stops = np.where(beh['teleport'] > 0)[0]\n    assert len(starts) == len(stops) and np.all(stops > starts), 'bad trial boundaries'\n    return beh, starts, stops\n\n\ndef read_fluorescence(f):\n    \"\"\"Pooled (ncells, nframes) F and Fneu over all imaging planes, iscell-curated.\"\"\"\n    seg = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation']\n    iscell = seg['iscell'][:, 0] > 0\n    planes = sorted(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence'].keys(),\n                    key=lambda p: int(p.replace('plane', '')))\n    Fs, Ns = [], []\n    for p in planes:\n        rois = f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/rois'][:]\n        keep = iscell[rois]\n        Fs.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Fluorescence/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n        Ns.append(f[f'{OPHYS_PATH}/Neuropil/{p}/data'][:][:, keep])\n    F = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Fs, axis=1).T)\n    Fneu = np.ascontiguousarray(np.concatenate(Ns, axis=1).T)\n    return F, Fneu, int(iscell.sum()), len(planes)\n\n\ndef convert_session(path, show_processing=False, outdir='/app'):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB session. Returns a dict with per-trial neural/input/output.\"\"\"\n    t0 = time.time()\n    timing = {}\n    with h5py.File(path, 'r') as f:\n        beh, starts, stops = read_behavior(f)\n        scene = f['identifier'][()].decode().split('/')[-1]\n        subject = f['general/subject/subject_id'][()].decode()\n        session_id = f['general/session_id'][()].decode()\n        region = f['general/optophysiology/ImagingPlane/location'][()].decode()\n        # ImagingPlane/imaging_rate is the total scan rate (31.0 Hz for the two\n        # 2-plane mice m17/m18); the effective per-plane sampling rate -- which is\n        # what every timeseries in the file is sampled at -- is 15.5078125 Hz for\n        # every session.  Derive it from the frame timestamps.\n        frame_rate = float(1.0 / np.median(np.diff(beh['time'])))\n        t1 = time.time()\n        timing['read_behavior'] = t1 - t0\n        F, Fneu, n_iscell, nplanes = read_fluorescence(f)\n    t2 = time.time()\n    timing['read_fluorescence'] = t2 - t1\n\n    ntrials = len(starts)\n\n    # ---- per-trial behaviour -----------------------------------------------------\n    pos_tr = [beh['position'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    speed_tr = [beh['speed'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    lick_tr = [beh['lick'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    rz_tr = [beh['reward_zone'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    rew_tr = [beh['reward'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    env_tr = [beh['environment'][s:e] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n    time_tr = [beh['time'][s:e] - beh['time'][s] for s, e in zip(starts, stops)]\n\n    # behavior.get_trial_types\n    isreward = np.array([float(np.any(r > 0) and np.any(z > 0))\n                         for r, z in zip(rew_tr, rz_tr)])\n    env = np.array([np.unique(e)[0] for e in env_tr])\n    for e in env_tr:\n        assert len(np.unique(e)) == 1, 'environment changes within a trial'\n\n    # behavior.get_reward_zones\n    labels = get_reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials)\n\n    # behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error -> trials to drop\n    lick_error = np.array([(l > 2).sum() / len(l) > LICK_CORRECTION_THR for l in lick_tr])\n\n    # ---- neural ------------------------------------------------------------------\n    dff_trials = compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops)\n    t3 = time.time()\n    timing['dff'] = t3 - t2\n\n    is_int, speed_r = find_putative_interneurons(dff_trials, [v.astype(np.float64)\n                                                             for v in speed_tr])\n    keep_cells = ~is_int\n    dff_trials = [d[keep_cells] for d in dff_trials]\n    t4 = time.time()\n    timing['interneurons'] = t4 - t3\n\n    n_nonfinite = int(sum(np.sum(~np.isfinite(d)) for d in dff_trials))\n    if n_nonfinite:\n        warnings.warn(f'{os.path.basename(path)}: {n_nonfinite} non-finite dF/F values '\n                      f'set to 0')\n        dff_trials = [np.nan_to_num(d, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)\n                      for d in dff_trials]\n\n    # ---- assemble ----------------------------------------------------------------\n    neural, inputs, outputs, kept_trials = [], [], [], []\n    for t in range(ntrials):\n        if lick_error[t]:\n            continue\n        T = len(pos_tr[t])\n        lo, hi = REWARD_ZONE_COORDS[labels[t]]\n        dist = reward_zone_distance(pos_tr[t], lo, hi)\n\n        inp = np.empty((4, T), dtype=np.float32)\n        inp[0] = time_tr[t]\n        inp[1] = env[t]\n        inp[2] = t                                  # original index within the session\n        inp[3] = isreward[t - 1] if t > 0 else 0.0  # no known preceding lap for trial 0\n\n        out = np.empty((6, T), dtype=np.int8)\n        out[0] = bin_reward_distance(dist)\n        out[1] = bin_position(pos_tr[t])\n        out[2] = bin_speed(speed_tr[t])\n        out[3] = (lick_tr[t] > 0).astype(np.int8)\n        out[4] = 'ABC'.index(labels[t])\n        out[5] = int(isreward[t])\n\n        neural.append(dff_trials[t])\n        inputs.append(inp)\n        outputs.append(out)\n        kept_trials.append(t)\n\n    timing['total'] = time.time() - t0\n    info = dict(\n        path=path, subject=subject, session_id=session_id, scene=scene,\n        region=region, frame_rate=frame_rate, nplanes=nplanes,\n        n_iscell=n_iscell, n_interneurons=int(is_int.sum()),\n        nneurons=int(keep_cells.sum()), ntrials_raw=ntrials,\n        ntrials=len(neural), n_lick_error=int(lick_error.sum()),\n        n_nonfinite=n_nonfinite, kept_trials=kept_trials,\n        reward_rate=float(isreward.mean()), timing=timing,\n    )\n\n    if show_processing:\n        plot_processing(path, beh, starts, stops, F, Fneu, dff_trials, keep_cells,\n                        labels, isreward, env, lick_error, neural, inputs, outputs,\n                        kept_trials, info, outdir)\n\n    return dict(neural=neural, input=inputs, output=outputs, info=info)\n\n\n# f\"{info['subject']}_ses-{info['session_id']}\"\n    ntr = len(starts)\n    demo = [t for t in range(ntr) if t in kept_trials][:4]\n    if len(demo) < 4:\n        demo = list(range(min(4, ntr)))\n\n    fig, axes = plt.subplots(7, 1, figsize=(18, 22))\n\n    # (1) session overview: position with trial windows\n    ax = axes[0]\n    n_show = min(len(beh['position']), stops[min(9, ntr - 1)] + 200)\n --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n_WORKER_ARGS = {}\n\n\ndef _worker(path):\n    try:\n        return convert_session(path, **_WORKER_ARGS)\n    except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover\n        import traceback\n        traceback.print_exc()\n        raise RuntimeError(f'failed on {path}: {exc}')\n\n\ndef _init(kwargs):\n    _WORKER_ARGS.update(kwargs)\n\n\ndef main():\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)\n    ap.add_argument('outfile')\n    ap.add_argument('--full', action='store_true', default=True,\n                    help='process all sessions (default)')\n    ap.add_argument('--sample', action='store_true',\n                    help='process only 2 sessions for testing')\n args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_ROOT, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n    if args.sample:\n        # one small single-plane session and one large 2-plane session\n    plot_files = set(files[:2]) if args.show_processing else set()\n    t_start = time.time()\n\n    results = []\n    if args.workers > 1 and not args.show_processing:\n        with Pool(args.workers, res, t_start)\n    else:\n        for i, path in enumerate(files):\n            res = convert_session(path, show_processing=path in plot_files)\n            results.append(res)\n            _report(i, int(r['info']['session_id'])))\n\n    subjects = sorted({r['info']['subject'] for r in results},\n                      key=lambda s: int(s[1:]))\n    subject_idx = dtype=np.int64) for r in results]\n\n    frame_rates = np.array([r['info']['frame_rate'] for r in results])\n    assert np.allclose(frame_rates, frame_rates[0], rtol=1e-6), \\\n        f'inconsistent          'Head-fixed mice ran laps on a 450 cm virtual linear track (ENV 1 or ENV 2) '\n                'containing a hidden 50 cm reward zone at one of three locations '\n                '(A 80-130 cm, B 200-250 cm, C 320-370 cm). Teleport periods are **excluded** from dF/F (`keep_teleports=False`).\n- Place-cell/spatial analyses exclude samples with speed <2 cm/s. **We do not apply this filter**,\n  because speed (including the \"<2 cm/s\" class) is one of the decoder outputs and removing samples\n  would break the continuous time base required by the decoder task.\n\n### Curation Steps\n**Neuron curation rules**\n1. `iscell[:,0] == 1` — suite2p + manual curation (removes ROIs with multiple somata/dendrites,\n   no transients, over-expression, putative interneurons).\n2. Exclude putative interneurons: Pearson `r(dF/F, speed) > 0.5` over all in-trial samples.\n\n**Trial curation rules**\n1. Trials are `[trial_start_inds[t], teleport_inds[t])`.\n2. Trials with lick-sensor error (>30% of samples with cumulative lick count >2) are removed\n   (the reference sets their licks to NaN; because lick is a decoder *output* and NaNs are\n   forbidden, we drop those trials entirely — 81 trials, 0.66%).\n\n### Decoders Trained (in the paper)\n| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n|---|---|\n| Reward-relative (circular) position from RR/TR/non-RR cells | reported as a **cosine \"decode score\"** (1 = perfect, 0 = chance), ≈0.5–0.8 for the example session (Fig. 3a,b), and as a z-score vs. circular-shift shuffles. No classification accuracies are reported, so there is no directly comparable number for the categorical decoder used here. |\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Discrepancies Found\n| Topic | Code says | Data shows | Paper says | Resolution |\n|-------|-----------|------------|------------|------------|\n| Total trials | `len(sess.trial_start_inds)` | 12,216 over 152 NWB sessions | 12,376 over \"11 switch mice\" | m11 was not *imaged* on days 1–2, so DANDI has 152 sessions; 11×14 = 154 sessions of behaviour exist. 12,376 − 12,216 = 160 = exactly 2 sessions × 80 trials ⇒ the paper's denominator includes m11's two unimaged behaviour days. first trial of a session → 0 | `behavior.get_trial_types` | constant within trial |\n| `position` + scene-derived reward zone | `output[0]` `reward_zone_distance` | signed distance to nearest point of the active zone, then 7 bins | `behavior.get_reward_zones` | time-varying |\n| `position` | `output[1]` `position` | 5 bins of 90 cm | — | time-varying |\n| `speed` | `output[2]` `speed` | 5 bins (<2, 2–10, 10–20, 20–40, >40 cm/s) | — | time-varying |\n| `lick` | `output[3]` `lick` | `lick>0 → 1` | `behavior.lickrate`, `lickrate_PETH` | time-varying |\n| scene name (+ `change_trial=30`) | `output[4]` `reward_zone_location` | A→0, B→1, C→2 | `behavior.get_reward_zones` | per-trial, broadcast over time |\n| `Reward` + `reward_zone` | `output[5]` `reward_outcome` | `any(reward) & any(rzone)` | `behavior.get_trial_types` | per-trial, broadcast over time |\n| `general/subject/subject_id` | `subjects` / `subject_idx` | `m3 … m19` | — | |\n| `ImagingPlane/location` | `brain_regions` | `['CA1']` | — | all neurons index 0 |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Neural signal = dF/F computed with the reference `preprocessing.dff`.**\n   The paper's core processed signal is dF/F (maximin baseline within each trial, neuropil\n   subtraction with coefficient 0.7, 2-sample Gaussian smoothing). It is *not* in the NWB files, so\n   it is recomputed exactly as in `utilities.multi_anim_sess` → `preprocessing.dff`.\n   The NWB's `Deconvolved` array is suite2p's `spks` computed from **raw F** (no neuropil\n   correction, no per-trial maximin baseline), i.e. *not* the \"events\" the paper uses, so it is\n   not used. We also do **not** re-deconvolve the dF/F, because that step needs the per-session\n   suite2p `ops['tau']`, which is not present in the NWB export; introducing a guessed kernel would\n   be a worse match to the reference than using the dF/F the paper itself defines.\n2. **Trial window = `[trial_start_idx, teleport_idx)`** — exactly the on-track samples, matching\n   every behavioural function in the reference (`get_trial_types`, `lickrate_PETH`,\n   `correct_lick_sensor_error`). `pp.dff` internally slices `start-1:stop-1`, so we pass\n   `trial_starts+1`/`teleports+1` to it, giving the identical sample window for neural and\n   behavioural streams (no temporal misalignment).\n3. **Temporal alignment at trial start**, `off_start = 0.0`, `off_end = None` (trials have\n   different lengths; a trial runs until the teleport, which is when track position ends).\n   No resampling: time bin = the native imaging frame, 1000/15.5078125 = **64.4839 ms**.\n4. **Neuron curation**: `iscell==1`, then exclude putative interneurons (`r(dF/F, speed) > 0.5`),\n   both directly from the reference pipeline.\n5. **Trial curation**: drop the 81 lick-sensor-error trials (the reference NaNs their licks; NaN is\n   not representable in a categorical output). No other trial exclusions — every trial has valid\n   VR data (`scanning == 1`), a single environment value, and ≥96 frames.\n6. **No speed threshold.** The paper excludes <2 cm/s samples for spatial analyses; the decoder task\n   explicitly requires a \"<2 cm/s\" speed class, so all samples are kept. Documented deviation.\n7. **Reward zone from the scene name** (`behavior.get_reward_zones` logic) rather than from the\n   observed rzone-entry position, because the zone is defined even on trials where the animal never\n   enters it. Validated against the data (0/12,216 mismatches).\n8. **`prev_trial_outcome` for the first trial of a session = 0.** There is no previous trial inside\n   the recording (the 30 pre-session warm-up trials are not in the data), so \"no known preceding\n   reward\" is encoded as 0. This affects 152/12,135 = 1.25% of trials.\n9. **Trial number keeps its original within-session index** even when an earlier trial has been\n   removed by lick-sensor curation, so that the input is the true ordinal position in the session\n   and `prev_trial_outcome` refers to the true preceding lap.\n10. **Discretisation** exactly as specified by the decoder task (bin edges in Step 6).\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [x] Total trials = 12,216; lick-error trials at thr 0.3 = 81 (paper: 81)\n- [x] Reward rate 84.7% (paper: ~85%)\n- [x] Cells/session min = 155 (paper: 155–2172); switch-day mean 969.5 ± 465.8 (paper: 954 ± 453)\n- [x] Scene-derived reward zone vs. measured rzone-entry position: 0/12,216 mismatches\n- [ ] Interneuron exclusion rate ≈ 0.42 ± 0.85% of cells (paper)\n- [ ] dF/F in a plausible range, no NaN/Inf\n- [ ] Position within trials spans ~0–450 cm; distance-to-reward bin 3 (=0 cm) occupies ≈50/450 of\n      the track samples\n- [ ] Spot-check raw NWB values against the converted pickle (`np.allclose`) for neural, input and\n      output streams\n- [ ] Trial/session/subject counts in the converted file match the scan\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py`. Run as\n`python -u /app/convert_data.py <outpickle> [--full|--sample] [--show-processing] [--workers N]`.\n\nStructure:\n- `get_reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials)` — re-implementation of `behavior.get_reward_zones`\n  (only the label is needed; coordinates come from `REWARD_ZONE_COORDS`).\n- `compute_dff_trials(F, Fneu, starts, stops)` — re-implementation of `preprocessing.dff` for the\n  single-channel, `neuropil_method='subtract'`, `baseline_method='maximin'`, `keep_teleports=False`\n  branch that `utilities.multi_anim_sess` uses. Runs per trial (mathematically identical to the\n  reference, which builds a full NaN-padded array and then loops over the same trial windows).\n- `find_putative_interneurons` — `spatial.is_putative_interneuron(method='speed', r_thresh=0.5)`,\n  computed from streaming per-trial accumulators rather than materialising the concatenation.\n- `bin_reward_distance` / `bin_position` / `bin_speed` / `reward_zone_distance` — the decoder-task\n  discretisation.\n- `read_behavior`, `read_fluorescence` — NWB loading (multi-plane pooling, `iscell` curation,\n  reconstruction of the per-frame reward binary from the `Reward` event timestamps).\n- `convert_session` — one session; `plot_processing` — the `--show-processing` figure.\n- `main` — multiprocessing over sessions, assembly, summary statistics, pickling.\n\nCode inefficiencies identified:\n- Naively slicing `F[s:e, keep].T` per trial does a fancy-index + transpose copy on every trial.\n- Building the full NaN-padded `(ncells, nframes)` dF/F array (as the reference does) wastes the\n  ~15% of frames in teleport periods and doubles peak memory.\n- Concatenating all trials' dF/F to correlate with speed for the interneuron test doubles memory.\n\nCode speedups added:\n- ROIs are `iscell`-filtered **before** the transpose, once per session\n  (`np.ascontiguousarray(F[:, keep].T)`), so per-trial slices are cheap views.\n- dF/F is computed directly into per-trial arrays (no NaN padding).\n- `find_putative_interneurons` streams sufficient statistics (Σx, Σx², Σxy, …) per trial.\n- 16 worker processes over sessions (`multiprocessing.Pool.imap`).\n- float64 only inside the per-trial dF/F arithmetic (matching the reference, which uses float64),\n  float32 for everything stored.\nResult: **full conversion of 152 sessions in 39 s** (of which 11 s is writing the 9.5 GB pickle).\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing`\n(sessions: m11 ses-03, a small single-plane session; list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\\n\\n### Consistency requirements\\n\\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\\n- Loading of data\\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\\n\\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \\n\\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \\n\\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\\n\\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \\n\\n---\\n\\n## Conversion Workflow\\n\\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Each step has explicit completion criteria. Do not proceed to the next step until the current step is complete. This helps you and the user track progress.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 0: Setup and Initialization\\n\\n**Goal**: Set up the working environment and create the notes file.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. **FIRST**: Create `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` with the template structure shown at the end of this document\\n2. Important functions from exploring the reference code\\n  - Dataset structure from exploring the dataset\\n  - Analysis described in the reference texts\\n- Note and investigate any discrepancies\\n- In particular, look for discrepancies in:\\n  - Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\\n- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\\n- Write efficient code:\\n  - Vectorize loops\\n  - Avoid unnecessary file I/O\\n  - Use parallel processing if beneficial\\n  - Print timing information to find bottlenecks\\n- Plots for `--show-processing` mode should visually convince the user that every step of the conversion is correct.\\n  - There are no temporal misalignments\\n  - Discretization of continuous outputs is correct\\n- Write clear, well-documented functions\\n- Handle missing data appropriately (consult references, use sensible defaults, document)\\n- Validate data shapes and types at each step\\n- Include sanity checks (e.g., trial counts match across arrays)\\n\\n**Done when**: `/app/convert_data.py` exists and runs efficiently without errors.\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 7 until `/app/convert_data.py` exists and you have updated Step 6 in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the conversion on a small sample before processing the full dataset.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \\n5. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_full_out.txt`. \\n6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \\n7. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `/app/verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- `/app/converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `/app/verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 9\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `/app/converted_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Address each warning by either fixing its cause or verifying it that it is not possible to fix it. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\\n- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\\n- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\\n- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \\n- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \\n- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \\n- Document your sanity checks to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\\n- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \\n- For each major processing step — (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction — identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \\n- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \\n- Fix any mismatches. \\n- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\\n\\n**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\\n- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference paper. \\n- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \\n- Fix any discovered issues. \\n- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\\n- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \\n- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\nWrite a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 10\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\\n\\n**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Do not skip or abbreviate. Do not proceed to Step 12 until this step is completely finished.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --plot-samples 2>&1 | tee /app/train_decoder_full_out.txt`. If the GPU does not have sufficient RAM for the network training, use the flag `--cpu` to specify to use the CPU to train. \\n2. **Wait for complete execution** — this may take significant time for large datasets\\n3. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\\n4. **Check accuracy**: High accuracy is an indicator that data conversion has been done correctly. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the paper. \\n\\n**Done when**: \\n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 11\\\" with a table of accuracies\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Edits can now be easily compared and merged across branches, for instance, because notebook outputs and formatting are excluded or converted to plain text. For instance, when determining which cells are place cells, we compare the spatial information of each cell to the distribution of spatial information scores within the animal resulting from 100 shuffles per cell of position relative to neural activity. Since the shuffle is randomly generated each time the code is run, there will always be +/- a few cells that pass as place cells/not place cells each time, for the cells that have borderline significant spatial information (consider the case where a cell has p=0.04 on one run of the shuffle and p=0.05 on another run). A similar type of shuffle criterion is used to define reward-relative cells. \\n\\nThis results in some stochasticity, such that if a user runs the whole pipeline from raw or early-level pre-processed data to plotting figures, they will not necessarily generate the __exact__ same plot that is in the paper. Importantly, however, the overall result should be the same, just perhaps with a slightly different n of included cells or slightly different p-value (but same order of magnitude) from the result reported in the paper, as the paper results came from a particular iteration of all of these randomized computations. We view this as a positive scientifically, because population-level results do not depend on the inclusion or exclusion of a handful of cells. \\n\\nTo replicate the plots exactly as they are in the paper, the post-processed version of the data used for the manuscript will be provided. \\n=====DOCS preprocessing=====\\n# Preprocessing guide\\n\\nThis is meant to serve as a reference for how data were preprocessed from the raw imaging/VR files to the several levels of data structures used for analysis.\\n\\nAll file paths are written as if we are in the current repo, i.e. the pip installable modules will be listed as `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\nIf I say \\\"module\\\" I mean to look for a .py file in `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\n\\n### Directory structure\\n\\n* data_root: e.g. `/data/`\\n    * `2P_Data` (sometimes omitted locally)\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyyy\\n                * scene: e.g. Env1_LocationA\\n                    * If you copied the scanbox files locally, they would be here as .sbx and .mat alongside the below directory\\n                    * session + scan directory: e.g. Env1_LocationA_002_001; session (index of Unity VR file) = 002, scan number (index of scan in Scanbox) = 001\\n                        * suite2p\\n                            * plane0 (plane1, combined, etc if multiplane)\\n    * `VR_Data`\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyy\\n                * SQLite files: scene_session.sqlite, e.g. Env1_LocationA_2.sqlite\\n\\n### Order of operations:\\n\\n0. Update `./src/reward_relative/sessions_dict.py` with the metadata from each recording session, with one dictionary entry per animal in either `single_plane` or `multi_plane`\\n    1. Include date, scene name, session, scan number, experiment day (1-indexed)\\n1. Extract binaries, run suite2p to do motion correction and find ROIs\\n    1. In `./notebooks/suite2p_notebooks`, duplicate an existing notebook and rename for the current animal\\n    2. Manually edit with the sessions you want to process\\n    3. Manually edit any suite2p parameters you want to change (for example, if you think the expression was weak, you could lower threshold_scaling from 1 to 0.6-0.8)\\n    4. For Scanbox data, running the main notebook cell will convert the .sbx files to .h5 and then run suite2p\\n2. Curate cells in the suite2p GUI\\n    1. `iscell.npy` is automatically updated and saved during curation\\n    2. Be sure to backup curated data so you don't lose all that work!\\n3. Copy VR_Data to the local machine with rclone or similar\\n4. Make `sess` class which aligns imaging data to Unity VR data.\\n    1. The code for the class object itself is in a separate repo, `TwoPUtils` \\n    2. The function that actually interpolates/aligns VR data to the slower imaging frame rate is `vr_align_to_2P` in `TwoPUtils/preprocessing.py`\\n    3. Use `./notebooks/make_session_pkl.ipynb` to make sess for each animal and list of experiment days that you want.\\n    4. `sess` pickles will be saved in `/data_root/sess/`\\n    5. Note `sess` does not contain deltaF/F -- this happens next, because it is more customizable. The idea is that you should only ever have to make the `sess` class once.\\n5. Make `multi_anim_sess` dictionary to collect and post-process sess across animals.\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`\\n    2. The core function `multi_anim_sess` in the `utilities` module runs functions to compute deltaF/F (dFF), calculates place cells from shuffles, and adds details like a trial set dictionary.\\n        1. The function that actually computes dFF is `dff` in the `preprocessing` module\\n    2. All of these are collected with the sess data for multiple animals on a single day, and stored in a dictionary where each top entry is an animal name. \\n    3. The notebook then saves this `multi_anim_sess` as a pickle so that we can work off a constant set of place cell IDs.\\n        1. TO-DO to free up disk space: save the sess pickle path as a pointer rather than re-saving the whole class inside multi_anim_sess\\n6. Align ROIs across days (can happen at any time after making sess)\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/Run_ROI_Aligner.ipynb`\\n    2. Saves matched ROI pair indices in `/data_root/sess/<animal>/roi_aligned_results.pkl`\\n7. For most analyses in Sosa, Plitt, Giocomo 2024, it is then necessary to create a `dayData` class for each experiment day, across animals.\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/make_multiDayData_class.ipynb`. `./reward_relative/dayData` has its own module with some helper functions. This `dayData` class contains computationally-intensive results like identifying reward-relative cells compared to a trial-by-trial shuffle of their activity.\\n8. Run remaining analyses and plot figures in `./notebooks` (more notebook figures will be posted as they are cleaned up for readability and documented).\\n\\n=====data_download=====\\n# Instructions to download data\\n\\nRequired hard drive space: \\n* 11 GB for multiDayData for switch days (days 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14)\\n* plus 22 GB for multiDayData for all experiment days (1 through 14)\\n* plus 200 GB for all of the multi_anim_sess pickles for each experiment day\\n\\nDownload from Figshare: \\n* [Preprocessed data i.e. multi_anim_sess](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.27098065)\\n* [Postprocessed data i.e. multiDayData](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.27138633)\\n    * where reward-relative cells have already been identified\\n* Both of these data structures are compatible with all the code in this repo\\n    \\nIf you want to download data in NWB format:\\n* [DANDI dataset](https://dandiarchive.org/dandiset/001361/0.250609.2249)\\n\\n[stdout]\\n# Sosa_et_al_2024\\nCode for analyses and figures in:  \\\\\\nSosa, Plitt, Giocomo. 2025. Edits can now be easily compared and merged across branches, for instance, because notebook outputs and formatting are excluded or converted to plain text. This is also very useful if you are trying out my notebooks but having trouble loading the .ipynb in your IDE of choice -- the .md file will let you start fresh with the same code, but without any saved outputs or cell runs.\\n\\n1. To install jupytext in your virtual environment:\\n```\\npip install jupytext --upgrade\\n```\\n\\n2. To synchronize a .ipynb with a .md:\\n```\\njupytext --set-formats ipynb,md --sync notebook.ipynb\\n```\\n\\n3. If you come across a .md without a .ipynb or you want to start fresh from the .md, just synchronize in the other direction:\\n```\\njupytext --set-formats ipynb,md --sync notebook.md\\n```\\n\\n\\n## A note about stochasticity in exact results\\n\\nMany of our computations, including thresholds for classifying individual cells, rely on shuffles or other randomized functions. For instance, when determining which cells are place cells, we compare the spatial information of each cell to the distribution of spatial information scores within the animal resulting from 100 shuffles per cell of position relative to neural activity. Since the shuffle is randomly generated each time the code is run, there will always be +/- a few cells that pass as place cells/not place cells each time, for the cells that have borderline significant spatial information (consider the case where a cell has p=0.04 on one run of the shuffle and p=0.05 on another run). A similar type of shuffle criterion is used to define reward-relative cells. \\n\\nThis results in some stochasticity, such that if a user runs the whole pipeline from raw or early-level pre-processed data to plotting figures, they will not necessarily generate the __exact__ same plot that is in the paper. Importantly, however, the overall result should be the same, just perhaps with a slightly different n of included cells or slightly different p-value (but same order of magnitude) from the result reported in the paper, as the paper results came from a particular iteration of all of these randomized computations. We view this as a positive scientifically, because population-level results do not depend on the inclusion or exclusion of a handful of cells. \\n\\nTo replicate the plots exactly as they are in the paper, the post-processed version of the data used for the manuscript will be provided. \\n=====DOCS preprocessing=====\\n# Preprocessing guide\\n\\nThis is meant to serve as a reference for how data were preprocessed from the raw imaging/VR files to the several levels of data structures used for analysis.\\n\\nAll file paths are written as if we are in the current repo, i.e. the pip installable modules will be listed as `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\nIf I say \\\"module\\\" I mean to look for a .py file in `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\n\\n### Directory structure\\n\\n* data_root: e.g. `/data/`\\n    * `2P_Data` (sometimes omitted locally)\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyyy\\n                * scene: e.g. Env1_LocationA\\n                    * If you copied the scanbox files locally, they would be here as .sbx and .mat alongside the below directory\\n                    * session + scan directory: e.g. Env1_LocationA_002_001; session (index of Unity VR file) = 002, scan number (index of scan in Scanbox) = 001\\n                        * suite2p\\n                            * plane0 (plane1, combined, etc if multiplane)\\n    * `VR_Data`\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyy\\n                * SQLite files: scene_session.sqlite, e.g. Env1_LocationA_2.sqlite\\n\\n### Order of operations:\\n\\n0. The notebook then saves this `multi_anim_sess` as a pickle so that we can work off a constant set of place cell IDs.\\n        1. Align ROIs across days (can happen at any time after making sess)\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/Run_ROI_Aligner.ipynb`\\n    2. Saves matched ROI pair indices in `/data_root/sess/<animal>/roi_aligned_results.pkl`\\n7. For most analyses in Sosa, Plitt, Giocomo 2024, it is then necessary to create a `dayData` class for each experiment day, across animals.\\n    1. This `dayData` class contains computationally-intensive results like identifying reward-relative cells compared to a trial-by-trial shuffle of their activity.\\n8. In their rawest form, they do NOT contain dF/F (dFF).\\n   1. dFF and trial_matrices (spatially binned data) can be added separately via methods of the sess class\\n   2. See make_session_pkl.ipynb\\n   3. Original code to construct the sess lives in the TwoPUtils repo\\n2. `multi_anim_sess`: computes dFF, calculates place cells, adds details like a trial set dictionary, and collects these and the sess data for multiple animals on a single day. Useful so you can work off a constant set of place cell IDs (since place cells are identified by their spatial information relative to a shuffle, which is stochastic for each run of the shuffle for cells that are borderline significant).\\n   1. See the [multi_anim_sess README](docs/multi_anim_sess_README.md) for a detailed description.\\n   1. See also `./notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`\\n3. `dayData`: class that takes multi_anim_sess as an input and performs additional computations like finding place cell peaks, computing circular distance between peaks relative to reward, computing correlation matrices, etc.\\n   1. Original sess data are not re-saved here, but a copy of the trial matrices are kept.\\n   2. `dayData.py` lives in the reward_relative modules\\n   3. Use `./notebooks/make_multiDayData_class.ipynb` to generate this class and save it as a pickle.\\n\\n## Preprocessing guide\\n\\n[Order of operations for running preprocessing](docs/preprocessing_guide.md)\\n\\n### Using jupytext for .ipynb version control\\n\\nJupyter notebooks are great for debugging and plotting, but sharing jupyter notebooks or merging them across branches with git can be a mess (because of the outputs). \\n\\n[Jupytext](https://jupytext.readthedocs.io/en/latest/install.html) is a useful tool that we can use to synchronize jupyter notebooks to markdown (.md) files for vastly improved version control. Edits can now be easily compared and merged across branches, for instance, because notebook outputs and formatting are excluded or converted to plain text. This is also very useful if you are trying out my notebooks but having trouble loading the .ipynb in your IDE of choice -- the .md file will let you start fresh with the same code, but without any saved outputs or cell runs.\\n\\n1. To install jupytext in your virtual environment:\\n```\\npip install jupytext --upgrade\\n```\\n\\n2. To synchronize a .ipynb with a .md:\\n```\\njupytext --set-formats ipynb,md --sync notebook.ipynb\\n```\\n\\n3. If you come across a .md without a .ipynb or you want to start fresh from the .md, just synchronize in the other direction:\\n```\\njupytext --set-formats ipynb,md --sync notebook.md\\n```\\n\\n\\n## A note about stochasticity in exact results\\n\\nMany of our computations, including thresholds for classifying individual cells, rely on shuffles or other randomized functions. For instance, when determining which cells are place cells, we compare the spatial information of each cell to the distribution of spatial information scores within the animal resulting from 100 shuffles per cell of position relative to neural activity. Since the shuffle is randomly generated each time the code is run, there will always be +/- a few cells that pass as place cells/not place cells each time, for the cells that have borderline significant spatial information (consider the case where a cell has p=0.04 on one run of the shuffle and p=0.05 on another run). A similar type of shuffle criterion is used to define reward-relative cells. \\n\\nThis results in some stochasticity, such that if a user runs the whole pipeline from raw or early-level pre-processed data to plotting figures, they will not necessarily generate the __exact__ same plot that is in the paper. Importantly, however, the overall result should be the same, just perhaps with a slightly different n of included cells or slightly different p-value (but same order of magnitude) from the result reported in the paper, as the paper results came from a particular iteration of all of these randomized computations. We view this as a positive scientifically, because population-level results do not depend on the inclusion or exclusion of a handful of cells. \\n\\nTo replicate the plots exactly as they are in the paper, the post-processed version of the data used for the manuscript will be provided. \\n=====DOCS preprocessing=====\\n# Preprocessing guide\\n\\nThis is meant to serve as a reference for how data were preprocessed from the raw imaging/VR files to the several levels of data structures used for analysis.\\n\\nAll file paths are written as if we are in the current repo, i.e. the pip installable modules will be listed as `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\nIf I say \\\"module\\\" I mean to look for a .py file in `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\n\\n### Directory structure\\n\\n* data_root: e.g. `/data/`\\n    * `2P_Data` (sometimes omitted locally)\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyyy\\n                * scene: e.g. Env1_LocationA\\n                    * If you copied the scanbox files locally, they would be here as .sbx and .mat alongside the below directory\\n                    * session + scan directory: e.g. Env1_LocationA_002_001; session (index of Unity VR file) = 002, scan number (index of scan in Scanbox) = 001\\n                        * suite2p\\n                            * plane0 (plane1, combined, etc if multiplane)\\n    * `VR_Data`\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyy\\n                * SQLite files: scene_session.sqlite, e.g. Env1_LocationA_2.sqlite\\n\\n### Order of operations:\\n\\n0. Update `./src/reward_relative/sessions_dict.py` with the metadata from each recording session, with one dictionary entry per animal in either `single_plane` or `multi_plane`\\n    1. Include date, scene name, session, scan number, experiment day (1-indexed)\\n1. Extract binaries, run suite2p to do motion correction and find ROIs\\n    1. In `./notebooks/suite2p_notebooks`, duplicate an existing notebook and rename for the current animal\\n    2. Manually edit with the sessions you want to process\\n    3. Manually edit any suite2p parameters you want to change (for example, if you think the expression was weak, you could lower threshold_scaling from 1 to 0.6-0.8)\\n    4. For Scanbox data, running the main notebook cell will convert the .sbx files to .h5 and then run suite2p\\n2. Curate cells in the suite2p GUI\\n    1. `iscell.npy` is automatically updated and saved during curation\\n    2. Be sure to backup curated data so you don't lose all that work!\\n3. Copy VR_Data to the local machine with rclone or similar\\n4. Make `sess` class which aligns imaging data to Unity VR data.\\n    1. The code for the class object itself is in a separate repo, `TwoPUtils` \\n    2. The function that actually interpolates/aligns VR data to the slower imaging frame rate is `vr_align_to_2P` in `TwoPUtils/preprocessing.py`\\n    3. Use `./notebooks/make_session_pkl.ipynb` to make sess for each animal and list of experiment days that you want.\\n    4. `sess` pickles will be saved in `/data_root/sess/`\\n    5. Note `sess` does not contain deltaF/F -- this happens next, because it is more customizable. The idea is that you should only ever have to make the `sess` class once.\\n5. Make `multi_anim_sess` dictionary to collect and post-process sess across animals.\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`\\n    2. The core function `multi_anim_sess` in the `utilities` module runs functions to compute deltaF/F (dFF), calculates place cells from shuffles, and adds details like a trial set dictionary.\\n        1. The function that actually computes dFF is `dff` in the `preprocessing` module\\n    2. All of these are collected with the sess data for multiple animals on a single day, and stored in a dictionary where each top entry is an animal name. \\n    3. The notebook then saves this `multi_anim_sess` as a pickle so that we can work off a constant set of place cell IDs.\\n        1. TO-DO to free up disk space: save the sess pickle path as a pointer rather than re-saving the whole class inside multi_anim_sess\\n6. Align ROIs across days (can happen at any time after making sess)\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/Run_ROI_Aligner.ipynb`\\n    2. Saves matched ROI pair indices in `/data_root/sess/<animal>/roi_aligned_results.pkl`\\n7. For most analyses in Sosa, Plitt, Giocomo 2024, it is then necessary to create a `dayData` class for each experiment day, across animals.\\n    1. Use `./notebooks/make_multiDayData_class.ipynb`. `./reward_relative/dayData` has its own module with some helper functions. This `dayData` class contains computationally-intensive results like identifying reward-relative cells compared to a trial-by-trial shuffle of their activity.\\n8. Run remaining analyses and plot figures in `./notebooks` (more notebook figures will be posted as they are cleaned up for readability and documented).\\n\\n=====data_download=====\\n# Instructions to download data\\n\\nRequired hard drive space: \\n* 11 GB for multiDayData for switch days (days 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14)\\n* plus 22 GB for multiDayData for all experiment days (1 through 14)\\n* plus 200 GB for all of the multi_anim_sess pickles for each experiment day\\n\\nDownload from Figshare: \\n* [Preprocessed data i.e. multi_anim_sess](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.27098065)\\n* [Postprocessed data i.e. multiDayData](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.27138633)\\n    * where reward-relative cells have already been identified\\n* Both of these data structures are compatible with all the code in this repo\\n    \\nIf you want to download data in NWB format:\\n* [DANDI dataset](https://dandiarchive.org/dandiset/001361/0.250609.2249)\",\n518:            \"stdout\": \"# Sosa_et_al_2024\\nCode for analyses and figures in:  \\\\\\nSosa, Plitt, Giocomo. 2025. Edits can now be easily compared and merged across branches, for instance, because notebook outputs and formatting are excluded or converted to plain text. For instance, when determining which cells are place cells, we compare the spatial information of each cell to the distribution of spatial information scores within the animal resulting from 100 shuffles per cell of position relative to neural activity. Since the shuffle is randomly generated each time the code is run, there will always be +/- a few cells that pass as place cells/not place cells each time, for the cells that have borderline significant spatial information (consider the case where a cell has p=0.04 on one run of the shuffle and p=0.05 on another run). A similar type of shuffle criterion is used to define reward-relative cells. \\n\\nThis results in some stochasticity, such that if a user runs the whole pipeline from raw or early-level pre-processed data to plotting figures, they will not necessarily generate the __exact__ same plot that is in the paper. Importantly, however, the overall result should be the same, just perhaps with a slightly different n of included cells or slightly different p-value (but same order of magnitude) from the result reported in the paper, as the paper results came from a particular iteration of all of these randomized computations. We view this as a positive scientifically, because population-level results do not depend on the inclusion or exclusion of a handful of cells. \\n\\nTo replicate the plots exactly as they are in the paper, the post-processed version of the data used for the manuscript will be provided. \\n=====DOCS preprocessing=====\\n# Preprocessing guide\\n\\nThis is meant to serve as a reference for how data were preprocessed from the raw imaging/VR files to the several levels of data structures used for analysis.\\n\\nAll file paths are written as if we are in the current repo, i.e. the pip installable modules will be listed as `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\nIf I say \\\"module\\\" I mean to look for a .py file in `./src/reward_relative`  \\\\\\n\\n### Directory structure\\n\\n* data_root: e.g. `/data/`\\n    * `2P_Data` (sometimes omitted locally)\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyyy\\n                * scene: e.g. Env1_LocationA\\n                    * If you copied the scanbox files locally, they would be here as .sbx and .mat alongside the below directory\\n                    * session + scan directory: e.g. Env1_LocationA_002_001; session (index of Unity VR file) = 002, scan number (index of scan in Scanbox) = 001\\n                        * suite2p\\n                            * plane0 (plane1, combined, etc if multiplane)\\n    * `VR_Data`\\n        * animal\\n            * date: dd_mm_yyy\\n                * SQLite files: scene_session.sqlite, e.g. Env1_LocationA_2.sqlite\\n\\n### Order of operations:\\n\\n0. Animals were originally named by indicator (i.e. GCAMP) and a number.\\n\\nIf you call the entry for a given animal, say \\\"GCAMP4\\\", it is a dictionary with keys: \\n```\\ndict_keys(['animal', 'sess', 'pc masks set0', 'pc masks set1', 'SI set0', 'SI set1', 'p set0', 'p set1', 'pc perms set0', 'pc perms set1', 'SI perms set0', 'SI perms set1', 'isreward', 'morph', 'dream', 'rzone', 'rz label', 'trial dict'])\\n```\\n\\n* `pc masks setx` is the boolean indicator telling you which unit/cell is a place cell or not in each trial set, where True means p<0.05 that it's a place cell\\n    * set0 is the 30 trials before the reward switch, set1 is all the trials after the reward switch\\n    * if there was no reward switch that day, set0 is the first half, set1 is the second half\\n    * I typically define \\\"overall\\\" place cells to be cells with significant spatial information (p<0.05, True) in set0 OR set1\\n* `sess` is a class created by the TwoPUtils repo with the neural and behavioral data from the session\\n* `SI`, `p` for each trial set are the spatial information per cell and p-value compared to shuffle per cell. The `perms` or shuffle information were not saved on figshare to reduce filesize.\\n* `is_reward` refers to a 1 x N trials binary array of whether a given trial was rewarded or not (1=rewarded, 0=omission trial)\\n* `morph` is a 1 x N trials binary array of which environment was active (0=Env 1, 1=Env 2)\\n* `dream` is something unused from another experiment, ignore it (it will be all zeros)\\n* `rzone` is a 2 x N trials array of the reward zone start and end coordinates, in cm\\n* `rz label` is a 1 x N trials array with text labels for which reward zone was active ('A', 'B', 'C')\\n* `trial dict` is a dictionary with entries `trial_set0` and `trial_set1`, which are each boolean arrays indicating which trials were included in which trial set.\\n\\nWithin multi_anim_sess['GCAMP4']['sess'], there are attributes: \\n```\\ndict_keys(['vr_data', 'trial_start_inds', 'teleport_inds', 'scan_info', 'n_planes', 'timeseries', 'trial_matrices', 'iscell', 'plane_per_cell', 's2p_ops', 's2p_stats', 'basedir_2P', 'basedir_VR', 'mouse', 'date', 'scene', 'session', 'scan_number', 'scanner', 'VR_only', 'scan_file', 'scanheader_file', 'vr_filename', 's2p_path', 'prompt_for_keys', 'verbose', 'basedir'])\\n```\\n\\n* `timeseries` is a dict containing the variables: dict_keys(['F', 'Fneu', 'licks', 'rewards', 'speed', 'events', 'dff'])\\n    *  each 'timeseries' entry is a cells x samples array, where each sample is a single imaging frame sampled at ~15.5 Hz (each frame is ~64.5 ms)\\n    * 'F' is the raw fluorescence of each cell ROI\\n    * 'Fneu' is the fluorescence in a small \\\"donut\\\" around the ROI that is subtracted in preprocessing before you get \\\"dff\\\"\\n    * 'dff' is delta F/F\\n    * 'events' is the deconvolved spike-like activity from 'dff' (but it's not really a spike rate, it just gets rid of the asymmetric smoothing of the calcium kernel)\\n    * 'licks' are a cumulative lick count in each frame, so in my behavior code anything >1 gets set to 1 to be able to convert it accurately to a rate when I want to convert it to Hz per position bin or time bin\\n    * 'rewards' is just a binary at the sample where reward was delivered\\n    * 'speed' is an actual smoothed running speed in cm/s for each sample.\\n* `trial_matrices` are the spatially binned versions of timeseries, in bins of 10 cm, from 0 to 450 cm (not including the teleport zone). Shape: trials x position bins x cells.\\n* `trial_start_inds` is a 1 x N trials array of the sample index for the start of each trial (i.e. the start of the track)\\n* `teleport_indices` is a 1 x N trials array of the sample index for the start of the teleport period (i.e. the end of the track)\\n* `vr_data` is a Pandas dataframe of VR behavior data converted from the sqlite files output by Unity and already synchronized with the imaging data\\n\\nThe sess class, which aligns the VR data to the imaging data, is generated by [preprocessing.vr_align_to_2P](https://github.com/GiocomoLab/TwoPUtils/blob/00b6589e5afea4cfe2347557b0a2450d9673c435/TwoPUtils/preprocessing.py#L124) in the [TwoPUtils](https://github.com/GiocomoLab/TwoPUtils/tree/main) repo. it includes mice m2, m3, m4, m6, m7, m10, m11, m12, m12, m13, m14, m15, m17, m18, m19. 2,3,4,7,11,12,13,14,15,17,18,19 learned the reward zone switch task.\\n* it contains data from experiment day 3 (the 1st switch day)\\n* place cells were identified taking neural activity at running speeds >2 cm/s\\n* 100 permutations were used for place cell significance calculations\\n* the dF/F baseline was calculated using a `maximin` filter\\n* deconvolved calcium `events` were used to define place cells\\n\\nEach pickle file is a collection of dictionaries, with a key for each animal, plus a key for the `params` used to define place cells. Animals were originally named by indicator (i.e. GCAMP) and a number.\\n\\nIf you call the entry for a given animal, say \\\"GCAMP4\\\", it is a dictionary with keys: \\n```\\ndict_keys(['animal', 'sess', 'pc masks set0', 'pc masks set1', 'SI set0', 'SI set1', 'p set0', 'p set1', 'pc perms set0', 'pc perms set1', 'SI perms set0', 'SI perms set1', 'isreward', 'morph', 'dream', 'rzone', 'rz label', 'trial dict'])\\n```\\n\\n* `pc masks setx` is the boolean indicator telling you which unit/cell is a place cell or not in each trial set, where True means p<0.05 that it's a place cell\\n    * set0 is the 30 trials before the reward switch, set1 is all the trials after the reward switch\\n    * if there was no reward switch that day, set0 is the first half, set1 is the second half\\n    * I typically define \\\"overall\\\" place cells to be cells with significant spatial information (p<0.05, True) in set0 OR set1\\n* `sess` is a class created by the TwoPUtils repo with the neural and behavioral data from the session\\n* `SI`, `p` for each trial set are the spatial information per cell and p-value compared to shuffle per cell. The `perms` or shuffle information were not saved on figshare to reduce filesize.\\n* `is_reward` refers to a 1 x N trials binary array of whether a given trial was rewarded or not (1=rewarded, 0=omission trial)\\n* `morph` is a 1 x N trials binary array of which environment was active (0=Env 1, 1=Env 2)\\n* `dream` is something unused from another experiment, ignore it (it will be all zeros)\\n* `rzone` is a 2 x N trials array of the reward zone start and end coordinates, in cm\\n* `rz label` is a 1 x N trials array with text labels for which reward zone was active ('A', 'B', 'C')\\n* `trial dict` is a dictionary with entries `trial_set0` and `trial_set1`, which are each boolean arrays indicating which trials were included in which trial set.\\n\\nWithin multi_anim_sess['GCAMP4']['sess'], there are attributes: \\n```\\ndict_keys(['vr_data', 'trial_start_inds', 'teleport_inds', 'scan_info', 'n_planes', 'timeseries', 'trial_matrices', 'iscell', 'plane_per_cell', 's2p_ops', 's2p_stats', 'basedir_2P', 'basedir_VR', 'mouse', 'date', 'scene', 'session', 'scan_number', 'scanner', 'VR_only', 'scan_file', 'scanheader_file', 'vr_filename', 's2p_path', 'prompt_for_keys', 'verbose', 'basedir'])\\n```\\n\\n* `timeseries` is a dict containing the variables: dict_keys(['F', 'Fneu', 'licks', 'rewards', 'speed', 'events', 'dff'])\\n    *  each 'timeseries' entry is a cells x samples array, where each sample is a single imaging frame sampled at ~15.5 Hz (each frame is ~64.5 ms)\\n    * 'F' is the raw fluorescence of each cell ROI\\n    * 'Fneu' is the fluorescence in a small \\\"donut\\\" around the ROI that is subtracted in preprocessing before you get \\\"dff\\\"\\n    * 'dff' is delta F/F\\n    * 'events' is the deconvolved spike-like activity from 'dff' (but it's not really a spike rate, it just gets rid of the asymmetric smoothing of the calcium kernel)\\n    * 'licks' are a cumulative lick count in each frame, so in my behavior code anything >1 gets set to 1 to be able to convert it accurately to a rate when I want to convert it to Hz per position bin or time bin\\n    * 'rewards' is just a binary at the sample where reward was delivered\\n    * 'speed' is an actual smoothed running speed in cm/s for each sample.\\n* `trial_matrices` are the spatially binned versions of timeseries, in bins of 10 cm, from 0 to 450 cm (not including the teleport zone). Shape: trials x position bins x cells.\\n* `trial_start_inds` is a 1 x N trials array of the sample index for the start of each trial (i.e. the start of the track)\\n* `teleport_indices` is a 1 x N trials array of the sample index for the start of the teleport period (i.e. the end of the track)\\n* `vr_data` is a Pandas dataframe of VR behavior data converted from the sqlite files output by Unity and already synchronized with the imaging data\\n\\nThe sess class, which aligns the VR data to the imaging data, is generated by [preprocessing.vr_align_to_2P](https://github.com/GiocomoLab/TwoPUtils/blob/00b6589e5afea4cfe2347557b0a2450d9673c435/TwoPUtils/preprocessing.py#L124) in the [TwoPUtils](https://github.com/GiocomoLab/TwoPUtils/tree/main) repo. Please review this function carefully to understand how the VR data are pre-processed and written into sess.vr_data.\\n\\nIn multi_anim_sess['GCAMP4']['sess'].vr_data, there is one row per sample (imaging frame), and the relevant columns are:\\n* `time`: the timestamp of the sample, in the imaging frame rate (VR data have already been synchronized with imaging)\\n* `pos`: Animal's position in cm on a virtual linear track\\n* `trialnum`: trial number, where each trial is a lap of the track\\n* `dz`: delta in position from one sample to the next\\n* `speed`: the speed of the mouse in cm/s\\n* `lick`: lick detection by capacitive sensor; preprocessed cumulatively per imaging frame\\n* `reward`: a binary of when reward was delivered\\n* `rzone`: a binary flag of when the animal entered the reward zone; preprocessed cumulatively per imaging frame\\n* `morph`: the identity of the virtual environment (see above)\\n* `autoreward`: whether trial was automatically rewarded if the mouse failed to lick\\n* `tstart`: start of a trial, i.e. entry to the linear track\\n* `teleport`: end of a trial, i.e. entry to the linear track\\n* `scanning`: whether scanning occurred to collect imaging data (1 if scanning)\\n\\nAll other vr_data columns are unused or can safely be ignored.\\n\\nIn samples prior to when Unity started sending TTLs to the imaging computer to synchronize acquisition, `morph`, `trialnum`, and `scanning` have values set to -1, and `pos` is set to -500. \\n====dandiset====\\n# DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE LOCALLY.
